docs.title: Upgrading from 7.x
docs.text:
The 7.x search functions are removed. Prepare a query with find (or Substructure.smarts for SMARTS), pass search options with withOptions (Python with_options), whose chemistry field holds the chemistry settings, then search with match, matchAll or matchMany. Java matchMany takes a List<MolGraph>; new MolGraph(container) converts a CDK molecule.

7.x 8.0.0 Python smsd.find_mcs(a, b), smsd.mcs_result(a, b), smsd.mcs_rdkit(a, b) smsd.MCS.find(a).match(b), which accepts SMILES, MolGraph objects and RDKit molecules Python smsd.find_substructure(q, t), smsd.is_substructure(q, t) smsd.Substructure.find(q).match(t), then .found or .best Python smsd.batch_mcs(q, targets), smsd.batch_substructure(q, targets) smsd.MCS.find(q).match_many(targets), smsd.Substructure.find(q).match_many(targets) Python smsd.smarts_match(smarts, t), smsd.smarts_find_all(smarts, t), smsd.compile_smarts(smarts) smsd.Substructure.smarts(smarts), then .match(t).found or .match_all(t, limit) Java SearchEngine.findMCS(a, b), new SMSD(q, t, chem).findMCS() MCS.find(a).match(b) Java SearchEngine.findSubstructure(q, t), SearchEngine.isSubstructure(q, t, chem, ms), new SMSD(q, t, chem).isSubstructure() Substructure.find(q).match(t), then found() Java SearchEngine.batchSubstructure(q, targets, chem, ms), SearchEngine.findAllMCS, SearchEngine.findAllSubstructures matchMany(targets, numThreads) or matchAll(target, limit) on the prepared query Java SearchEngine.findMCSSmarts(smarts, target, chem, ms), new SMSD(smarts, target, chem) Substructure.smarts(pattern).match(target) C++ smsd::findMCS(a, b, ...), smsd::isSubstructure(q, t, ...), smsd::findSubstructure(q, t, ...) smsd::MCS::find(a).match(b), smsd::Substructure::find(q).match(t) C++ smsd::batch::batchMCS, smsd::batch::batchSubstructure, smsd::findAllMCS, smsd::findAllSubstructures matchMany(targets, numThreads) or matchAll(target, limit) on the prepared query Python timeout_ms= keyword arguments, Java SMSD.setMCSTimeoutMs(ms) and setSubstructureTimeoutMs(ms) withTimeout(ms) (Python with_timeout(ms)) on the prepared query Java artefact com.bioinceptionlabs:smsd with the CLI com.bioinceptionlabs:smsd for the library and com.bioinceptionlabs:smsd-cli for the command-line tool
  • Status and optimality: each result reports status (Completed, TimedOut, Cancelled or LimitReached; in Python SearchStatus.COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED or LIMIT_REACHED), optimal and complete. A stopped search may return a valid mapping without proving the optimum, and a capped matchAll (Python match_all) may prove it without listing every match, so check optimal and complete separately.
  • Java library and CLI: the library no longer brings picocli, jackson-databind or CDK modules such as cdk-smiles, cdk-data and the CDK file readers; projects that used them through smsd declare them. The self-contained CLI is smsd-cli-8.0.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar.
  • SMARTS: in C++, as in Java, uppercase bracket atoms such as [C] match aliphatic atoms only and lowercase ones aromatic atoms only; use [#6] or [C,c] for both. C++ reads [H], [2H] and [H+] as hydrogen atoms, and SMARTS beyond the size limits is rejected in every language.
  • Deprecated names keep working in 8.0.0, and Python names warn with DeprecationWarning. The warning, or the Java and C++ API documentation of the name, gives its replacement where one exists.

docs.title: SMARTS export
docs.text:
Java can write a portable SMARTS query from an MCS match or a whole molecular graph. SmartsWriter and SearchResult.Match.toSmarts are new in 8.1.0, while the published Java artefacts stay at 8.0.3 in this release, so compile this example against a Java source build:

import com.bioinception.smsd.core.MCS;
import com.bioinception.smsd.core.MolGraph;
import com.bioinception.smsd.core.SearchResult;
import com.bioinception.smsd.core.SmartsWriter;
import com.bioinception.smsd.core.Substructure;
import org.openscience.cdk.silent.SilentChemObjectBuilder;
import org.openscience.cdk.smiles.SmilesParser;

public class SmartsExportExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        SmilesParser parser = new SmilesParser(SilentChemObjectBuilder.getInstance());
        MolGraph query = new MolGraph(parser.parseSmiles("CCO"));
        MolGraph target = new MolGraph(parser.parseSmiles("CCCO"));
        MolGraph libraryMolecule = new MolGraph(parser.parseSmiles("CCOCC"));
        MCS.Options options = new MCS.Options();
        SearchResult common = MCS.find(query).withOptions(options).match(target);
        if (!common.found()) throw new IllegalStateException("No common substructure");
        String pattern = common.matches().get(0).toSmarts(query, options.chemistry);
        SearchResult hit = Substructure.smarts(pattern).match(libraryMolecule);
        if (!hit.found()) throw new IllegalStateException("Exported pattern did not match");
        System.out.println(pattern);
        System.out.println(SmartsWriter.toSmarts(query, options.chemistry));
    }
}

SmartsWriter.toSmarts(graph, chemistry) writes every atom and bond. A match writes only its selected atoms and common bonds, including an MCES match that leaves out a source bond. Ring and aromaticity flags retain their original graph context. The atom order follows the source indices; the text is deterministic for that numbering and is not canonical.

The writer supports element wildcards, formal charge including neutral atoms, isotope wildcards, strict or flexible aromaticity, bond-order modes and ring membership. As in molecule matching, isotope zero matches any isotope on the other side. The pattern is a subgraph query; it does not encode the induced MCIS objective, a search budget or an optimality proof.

Export throws IllegalArgumentException for stereo, tautomer-aware matching, complete-ring matching and strict ring-fusion matching. With flexible aromaticity and strict bond order, it also rejects a non-aromatic single or double bond between two aromatic atoms: the conditional resonance rule has no direct portable bond expression. Use supported options explicitly rather than silently dropping these constraints.

Portable output assumes molecular targets with consistent aromatic bond flags and bond orders. Contradictory source annotations supplied through a graph builder are rejected. Java SMARTS target preparation applies Daylight aromaticity. Strict export therefore also rejects selected aromatic flags that change under that model, including an uppercase Kekule benzene graph whose original flags are non-aromatic. This check uses the full source graph, preserving the context of selected atoms and bonds. Strict predicate parity with molecule matching requires library targets whose aromatic flags also agree with that preparation. At most 99 Java ring closures can be open at once; closure numbers are reused after they close.

docs.title: SMSD Pro user guide
docs.text: This guide shows how to search, compare and screen molecules with SMSD Pro 8.1.0. Most chapters work in Python; the last two cover the command-line tool, the Docker images and the C++ and Java libraries. Every Python example is a complete program that runs on a CPU-only machine, and the output shown below each one comes from running it on such a machine.

docs.title: Who the guide is for
docs.text: The guide is written for chemists, data scientists and software developers who need to find substructures and common substructures, compute fingerprints or screen a compound library. It assumes a working knowledge of Python and of SMILES, and no knowledge of how SMSD Pro searches. Each chapter starts from a task and shows the calls that carry it out. The reference pages list every function and option.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter What it covers Getting started Installation, a first substructure search and a first MCS search, and the conventions the other chapters rely on: reading a result, molecule input, atom numbering, default chemistry, time limits and threads Substructure search Prepared queries, one embedding or every embedding, many targets, prepared corpora, induced matching, chemistry options, hydrogen counts, limits, drawing a hit and R-group decomposition SMARTS queries Compiling a pattern, atom and bond primitives, recursive SMARTS, components, stereochemistry, the options that apply, SMARTS written from a molecule, limits and unsupported syntax Maximum common substructure MCIS and MCES, connected and fragment searches, proof and partial results, all optimal mappings, chemistry options, atom weights, reserved atoms, the common graph of a series, MCS similarity, export, drawing and tautomers Fingerprints and similarity Fingerprint families, count and configurable fingerprints, substructure keys and MACCS, many molecules at once, similarity coefficients, encodings and NumPy arrays Screening a library Choosing a route, preparing a library, similarity screens in memory and streamed from a file, an exact substructure screen, an MCS-similarity screen and saving the hits Packed fingerprint index Building and reopening an index file, threshold and nearest-neighbour searches, several queries in one pass, neighbours and pairs within the index, clustering, diverse selection and the file format CPU and GPU screening What runs where, checking the backend, installing the CUDA package, requesting or refusing the GPU, fallback and errors, and comparing the two devices Command line and containers The smsd command-line tool, SDF batch search, mapping export, exit status, the JSON report, the Docker images and the local molecular tools server C++ and Java The same searches in the C++ and Java libraries, and the differences between the languages

docs.title: How the chapters fit together
docs.text:
Read Getting started first: it installs the package and sets out the conventions that every later chapter assumes. The next three chapters cover the exact graph searches. Substructure search asks whether a query occurs whole inside a target, SMARTS queries describes the pattern language for the same searches, and Maximum common substructure finds the largest graph that two molecules share. Fingerprints and similarity turns molecules into fingerprints and compares them.

Screening a library brings these together: fingerprint screens narrow a library, and the exact searches decide which molecules match. Packed fingerprint index keeps a library's fingerprints in a file that is built once and searched in later sessions, and CPU and GPU screening explains which screening steps can run on an NVIDIA GPU. The last two chapters leave Python: Command line and containers runs single searches and SDF batch searches from a shell or a Docker image, and C++ and Java shows the same searches in the other libraries. After Getting started, each chapter can be read on its own, and the chapters link to each other where a topic continues.

docs.title: How the reference chapters are laid out
docs.text:
The chapters from Substructure search to Command line and containers follow a common pattern, so a detail is found in the same place in each:

  • what the feature does and when to use it;
  • how to use it, in the order the calls are usually made;
  • each kind of search or operation, with a runnable example and its output;
  • an options section that lists the methods, arguments or settings with their defaults;
  • notes on behaviour that is easy to miss;
  • see also, with links to related chapters and reference pages.

docs.title: Reading a result
docs.text:
Every search returns a SearchResult, and four of its fields say what the result proves:

  • status: why the search ended, one of COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED or LIMIT_REACHED;
  • optimal: whether the answer is proved; for a substructure search, a match exists or a completed search proved absence, and for an MCS, the maximum is proved;
  • complete: whether the search, or an enumeration of every match, ran to its end;
  • found: whether any match was returned.

An empty result proves absence only when status is COMPLETED and optimal is True. A search stopped by its time limit, node limit or cancellation proves nothing about what it did not find. Getting started describes the other fields and shows a stopped search.

docs.title: Running the examples
docs.text:
Install SMSD Pro 8.1.0 as shown in Getting started. Each Python block is a complete program: copy it into a file and run it with python. The values each program prints are also checked with assert statements. Programs that write files keep them in a temporary directory, and none downloads anything.

A few programs need more than the core package:

  • programs that use a packed fingerprint index, clustering or NumPy arrays need NumPy, from the numpy extra;
  • two programs take RDKit molecules, from the rdkit extra;
  • the GPU branches in CPU and GPU screening run only where the smsd-cuda package and a usable NVIDIA GPU are present, and the same programs take their CPU path everywhere else.

The C++ and Java programs build as described in C++ and Java. In a source checkout, scripts/check_examples.py runs every Python, C++ and Java block of this guide together with the other guides and the example notebooks; Check the documented examples gives the command.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
Notebook Topic Substructure and SMARTS search Molecule queries and SMARTS patterns on a small library of drugs and benzodiazepines: hydrogen counts, functional groups, enumeration, chemistry options, limits, corpus decisions and drawing a hit Maximum common substructure The two objectives, stopped searches, all mappings, chemistry rules, MCS similarity, SMARTS export and the common graph of a short series Fingerprints and similarity Every fingerprint family, the binary and count coefficients, configurable fingerprints and a similarity ranking of benzodiazepines Screening a library end to end Five screens of one library, clustering of the packed index and saving the hits to an SD file CPU and GPU screening The screening backend, automatic and requested GPU use, packed-index backends, fallback and a CPU and GPU comparison, with every cell able to run without a GPU MCS to a small library search A common graph turned into a SMARTS query, a library search, SVG highlighting, NumPy features, packed-index neighbours, Butina clustering and MaxMin selection

Open a notebook in Jupyter with a kernel that has SMSD 8.1.0 or later installed. The notebooks are saved without outputs, perform no downloads, remove any files they write and report when an optional package is missing. To run one in Colab, copy the setup cell of feature_search.ipynb to the top of the notebook and run it first; it installs an uploaded SMSD wheel.

docs.title: Reference pages
docs.text:
• Python guide: every function, class and option of the smsd package.
  • API reference: interfaces, options, proof and stopping status, input and output, fingerprints, adapters and GPU scope.
  • Search algorithms: search guarantees, result semantics and the differences between the languages.
  • Packed fingerprint corpora: the full packed-index API, its CPU and CUDA backends, ordering, work and memory.
  • Python examples: fingerprints, depiction, layout, stereo, files and R-groups, beyond searching.
  • C++ guide: the header-only C++ library.
  • Java guide: the Java library and its command-line tool.
  • Installation: platform requirements, downloads and source builds.

docs.title: Chemistry tools for AI assistants
docs.text: SMSD Pro 8.1.0 offers eight molecular tools that an AI assistant can call: maximum common substructure (MCS), substructure and SMARTS matching, fingerprints, similarity, small-list screening, standardisation and MCS depiction. The tools run on your own machine. They are served to an assistant by a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, smsd-mcp, and the same tools are available from Python as a registry with JSON schemas, so that your own code can offer them to a model or call them with no model at all. This chapter shows which route suits which task, what each tool takes and returns, how to start the server and connect a client, how to read a tool result, and the limits that keep each call bounded.

docs.title: Choose a route
docs.text:
Task Use Needs Model involved Give a desktop or terminal assistant the tools smsd-mcp, started by the assistant's MCP client The mcp extra Yours, through the client Offer the tools to a model API from your own program get_tool_definitions(provider) and call_tool(name, arguments) The core package Yours, through your code Run the tools from a script, a test or a workflow call_tool(name, arguments) The core package None Search a library, enumerate every match or set detailed chemistry The Python API: Substructure search, MCS, Screening The core package None

The tools are deliberately narrow: each call takes SMILES or SMARTS text, runs one bounded operation and returns a JSON-compatible dictionary. They suit questions about a few molecules at a time. For a library of thousands of molecules, a saved index or a GPU, use the Python API directly; the tools expose a subset of its options and cap every input.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool Required inputs Main optional inputs Returns find_mcs query_smiles, target_smiles objective (mcis or mces), connected, timeout_ms, node_limit, chemistry switches One common graph as matches, with status, optimal, complete, score and the budget used find_substructure query, target_smiles query_format (smarts or smiles), induced, timeout_ms, node_limit, chemistry switches One embedding of the query in the target, with the same proof fields search_smarts query_smarts, target_smiles max_matches (1 to 32), timeout_ms, node_limit, chemistry switches Every embedding up to max_matches, and truncated when the list stopped at the cap molecular_fingerprint smiles kind, fp_size, radius, path_length, counts values: set-bit positions, or position and count pairs molecular_similarity query_smiles, target_smiles metric (tanimoto, dice or cosine) and the fingerprint inputs score, the coefficient of the two fingerprints screen_molecules query_smiles, targets_smiles (a list) threshold, max_hits, offset and the fingerprint inputs One page of hits, each a target_index and Tanimoto score, with total_hits and next_offset standardise_molecule smiles remove_atom_maps; cleanup, largest_fragment, neutralise and canonical_tautomer, which need RDKit Canonical smiles, the backend used and the operations applied depict_mcs query_smiles, target_smiles The find_mcs inputs, width, height The find_mcs result plus svg, a drawing of the pair with the common atoms highlighted

The chemistry switches are match_stereo, complete_rings_only and ring_matches_ring_only, all off by default. Every other chemistry option keeps its default, described in Getting started, and each search result lists the options in force under chemistry. The fingerprint kind is one of ecfp, fcfp, circular, path, torsion or mcs; the Options section gives every default.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Install SMSD Pro with the mcp extra, which adds the MCP Python SDK. The server and the tool definitions need SMSD 8.1.0 or later and Python 3.12 or later:

python -m pip install "smsd[mcp]==8.1.0"
smsd-mcp
# Equivalent: python -m smsd.mcp_server

smsd-mcp takes no arguments. It talks to its client over standard input and output, writes diagnostics to standard error and opens no network port, so it is normally started by the client rather than from a shell; run by hand, it waits silently for protocol messages. Without the mcp extra it stops with ImportError: The MCP server requires the official SDK; install smsd[mcp].

To check an installation without an assistant, run mcp_stdio_client.py from the examples. It starts the server with the same interpreter, lists the eight tools and runs one find_mcs call through the protocol.

docs.title: Connect an MCP client
docs.text:
An MCP client needs two things: the command that starts the server and its arguments, which here are none. Many clients take a JSON entry of this form:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "smsd": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/smsd-mcp",
      "args": []
    }
  }
}

Give the absolute path that which smsd-mcp (on Windows, where.exe smsd-mcp) prints, because a desktop client may not search your shell's PATH; the path also fixes which Python environment, and so which SMSD version, the server uses. The server needs no API key and no environment settings. Once connected, the client lists the eight tools with their schemas, and the server also sends the client a short note on reading results: inspect status, optimal and complete, and do not read an unfinished search as a maximum or as proof of absence.

The configuration file, its location and the command that adds a server differ from client to client. Connecting AI assistants gives the exact steps for several desktop and terminal assistants and for an open model run on your own machine. Every result carries engine_version; use it to confirm the SMSD version, because some clients show the SDK's version for the server instead.

docs.title: Call the tools from Python
docs.text:
smsd.tool_definitions.call_tool(name, arguments) runs a tool locally, with the arguments as a dictionary of JSON values, and returns the same dictionary that the server sends to a client. It needs neither the mcp extra nor a model. The program below runs an MCS, two single substructure searches and a SMARTS enumeration:

from smsd.tool_definitions import call_tool

# MCS of N-methylacetamide and propanamide: atom-maximising, connected.
mcs = call_tool("find_mcs", {"query_smiles": "CC(=O)NC",
                             "target_smiles": "CCC(=O)N"})
print("find_mcs:", mcs["found"], mcs["status"], mcs["optimal"], mcs["complete"])
print("  atoms:", mcs["matches"][0]["atom_count"],
      "mapping:", mcs["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"])

# One embedding of a SMARTS pattern: a hydroxyl on an aromatic carbon.
hit = call_tool("find_substructure", {"query": "[OX2H]c",
                                      "target_smiles": "CC(C)(C)c1ccc(O)cc1"})
print("find_substructure:", hit["found"], hit["status"],
      hit["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"])

# The same call with a molecule as the query.
phenol = call_tool("find_substructure", {"query": "Oc1ccccc1",
                                         "target_smiles": "CC(C)(C)c1ccc(O)cc1",
                                         "query_format": "smiles"})
print("molecule query:", phenol["found"], len(phenol["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"]))

# Every embedding, up to max_matches: the three hydroxyls of glycerol.
every = call_tool("search_smarts", {"query_smarts": "[OX2H]",
                                    "target_smiles": "OCC(O)CO"})
print("search_smarts:", [m["atom_mapping"] for m in every["matches"]],
      "complete:", every["complete"], "truncated:", every["truncated"])

assert mcs["optimal"] and mcs["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"] == [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]
assert hit["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"] == [[0, 8], [1, 7]]
assert phenol["found"] and len(phenol["matches"][0]["atom_mapping"]) == 7
assert len(every["matches"]) == 3 and every["complete"] and not every["truncated"]

The program prints:

find_mcs: True COMPLETED True True
  atoms: 4 mapping: [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]
find_substructure: True COMPLETED [[0, 8], [1, 7]]
molecule query: True 7
search_smarts: [[[0, 0]], [[0, 3]], [[0, 5]]] complete: True truncated: False

Mappings are lists of [query_atom, target_atom] pairs, sorted by query atom, with zero-based atom numbers in the order of the input SMILES, as described in Atom numbering. find_substructure expects SMARTS unless query_format is "smiles". Each entry of matches also holds bond_mapping, fragments, atom_count and bond_count.

The tool functions can also be imported from smsd.mcp_server and called with keyword arguments; importing that module neither loads the SDK nor starts a server. Use call_tool for arguments that come from a model or a file: it checks the whole argument object against the schema first, as the server does.

docs.title: Read a tool result
docs.text:
A search result keeps the native fields of a SearchResult: found, status, optimal, complete, score, nodes_visited and elapsed_ms, with the same meanings as in Reading a result. It adds:

  • engine_version, the SMSD version that ran the call;
  • proof, which repeats optimal and complete with the scope native_search; it describes the search, and is not an independent chemical validation;
  • budget, the timeout_ms and node_limit in force, and chemistry, the chemistry options;
  • limits, the fixed input and output limits of the server;
  • timings, with wall_elapsed_ms from tool entry to just before the result is serialised, and native_search_ms.

The rule for an assistant is the rule for any search: a returned match is always a valid match, but found: false proves absence only when status is COMPLETED and optimal is true, and an MCS is proved maximum only when optimal is true. The program below shows a search stopped by its time limit, an enumeration stopped by its result cap, and the messages with which call_tool refuses bad arguments:

from smsd.tool_definitions import call_tool

anthracene = "c1ccc2cc3ccccc3cc2c1"

# A time limit of 0 stops the search at once: found=False proves nothing.
stopped = call_tool("find_substructure", {"query": "c1ccccc1",
                                          "target_smiles": anthracene,
                                          "timeout_ms": 0})
print("stopped:", stopped["found"], stopped["status"],
      stopped["optimal"], stopped["complete"])

# A result cap: the matches returned are real, but the list is not the whole.
capped = call_tool("search_smarts", {"query_smarts": "[OX2H]",
                                     "target_smiles": "OCC(O)CO",
                                     "max_matches": 2})
print("capped:", len(capped["matches"]), capped["status"],
      "complete:", capped["complete"], "truncated:", capped["truncated"])


def proves_absence(result):
    return (not result["found"] and result["status"] == "COMPLETED"
            and result["optimal"])


absent = call_tool("find_substructure", {"query": "[N]", "target_smiles": anthracene})
print("absence proved:", proves_absence(absent), "| after a stop:",
      proves_absence(stopped))

# Bad arguments are refused before any molecular work, with a short message.
for arguments in ({"query_smiles": "CCO"},
                  {"query_smiles": "CCO", "target_smiles": "CCN", "timeout_ms": 60000},
                  {"query_smiles": "CCO", "target_smiles": "CCN", "timeout_ms": "500"},
                  {"query_smiles": "CCO", "target_smiles": "CCN", "path": "a.sdf"},
                  {"query_smiles": "C1CC", "target_smiles": "CCN"}):
    try:
        call_tool("find_mcs", arguments)
    except ValueError as error:
        print("refused:", error)

assert stopped["status"] == "TIMED_OUT" and not stopped["complete"]
assert capped["status"] == "LIMIT_REACHED" and capped["truncated"]
assert proves_absence(absent) and not proves_absence(stopped)

The program prints:

stopped: False TIMED_OUT False False
capped: 2 LIMIT_REACHED complete: False truncated: True
absence proved: True | after a stop: False
refused: Missing required tool argument
refused: timeout_ms is outside its supported range
refused: timeout_ms must have JSON type integer
refused: Unknown tool argument
refused: Unclosed ring(s): 1

search_smarts reports a capped list as LIMIT_REACHED with complete: false and truncated: true; the matches it does return are valid, and optimal stays true because a match was found. Arguments are refused before any molecular work: unknown tools, unknown or missing arguments, JSON type changes such as a string for an integer, and values out of range each raise ValueError with a short message. A SMILES or SMARTS parse error also raises ValueError. Return that message to the model as the tool's answer, so that it can correct the call.

Fingerprint, similarity, screening and standardisation results are not searches. They report status: "COMPLETED", except a canonical tautomer chosen from a stopped enumeration, described below, and a proof whose scope names the operation and whose search_proof_applicable is false. A similarity score says how alike two fingerprints are; it is not an MCS size or a measure of biological activity.

docs.title: Fingerprints, similarity and screening
docs.text:
molecular_fingerprint returns the fingerprint as positions, which keeps the result small and readable. molecular_similarity compares two molecules with one coefficient, and screen_molecules scores a short list against one query and returns the hits at or above threshold one page at a time:

from smsd.tool_definitions import call_tool

# ECFP4 set bits in a 64-position fingerprint, then position/count pairs.
bits = call_tool("molecular_fingerprint", {"smiles": "OCCO", "fp_size": 64})
counts = call_tool("molecular_fingerprint", {"smiles": "OCCO", "fp_size": 64,
                                             "counts": True})
print("bits:", bits["values"])
print("counts:", counts["values"])
print("proof:", bits["proof"])

# Phenol against 2-methylphenol with each coefficient.
pair = {"query_smiles": "Oc1ccccc1", "target_smiles": "Cc1ccccc1O"}
for metric in ("tanimoto", "dice", "cosine"):
    score = call_tool("molecular_similarity", {**pair, "metric": metric})["score"]
    print(f"{metric}: {score:.3f}")

# A small list, two hits per page; next_offset leads to the next page.
library = ["Oc1ccccc1", "Cc1ccccc1O", "Nc1ccccc1", "CCO", "Oc1ccccc1", "c1ccccc1"]
request = {"query_smiles": "Oc1ccccc1", "targets_smiles": library,
           "threshold": 0.3, "max_hits": 2}
offset, pages = 0, []
while offset is not None:
    page = call_tool("screen_molecules", {**request, "offset": offset})
    pages.append([(hit["target_index"], round(hit["score"], 3)) for hit in page["hits"]])
    offset = page["next_offset"]
print("total hits:", page["total_hits"], "of", page["total_targets"])
for number, hits in enumerate(pages, 1):
    print(f"page {number}:", hits)

assert bits["values"] == [4, 5, 6, 27, 40, 62]
assert counts["values"] == [[4, 2], [5, 2], [6, 2], [27, 2], [40, 2], [62, 2]]
assert bits["proof"]["search_proof_applicable"] is False
assert pages == [[(0, 1.0), (4, 1.0)], [(1, 0.346)]]

The program prints:

bits: [4, 5, 6, 27, 40, 62]
counts: [[4, 2], [5, 2], [6, 2], [27, 2], [40, 2], [62, 2]]
proof: {'scope': 'fingerprint_generation', 'optimal': None, 'search_proof_applicable': False}
tanimoto: 0.346
dice: 0.514
cosine: 0.525
total hits: 3 of 6
page 1: [(0, 1.0), (4, 1.0)]
page 2: [(1, 0.346)]

screen_molecules scores every target, keeps those whose Tanimoto score is at least threshold, sorts them by descending score and then by input index, and returns at most max_hits from offset. next_offset is the offset of the next page, or None (null in JSON) on the last page, and truncated is true when the page does not hold the whole hit list. The screen always uses Tanimoto; metric belongs to molecular_similarity only. It runs on the CPU and is not an exact structure search. For a larger library, use the screens in Screening a library, which are not capped in this way.

docs.title: Standardisation and depiction
docs.text:
standardise_molecule by default parses the molecule and writes canonical SMILES. It changes the representation only: charges, fragments, isotopes, stereochemistry and atom maps are kept, and remove_atom_maps is a separate switch. depict_mcs runs the same search as find_mcs and adds an SVG drawing of the pair:

from smsd.tool_definitions import call_tool

# The default changes the representation only: charges and fragments stay.
salt = call_tool("standardise_molecule", {"smiles": "[Na+].[O-]C(=O)c1ccccc1"})
print("smiles:", salt["smiles"], "| backend:", salt["backend"])
print("operations:", salt["operations"],
      "| chemical transformations:", salt["chemical_transformations"])

mapped = call_tool("standardise_molecule", {"smiles": "[CH3:1][OH:2]",
                                            "remove_atom_maps": True})
print("atom maps removed:", mapped["smiles"], mapped["operations"])

# The MCS of phenol and aniline, with the search result and a drawing.
drawing = call_tool("depict_mcs", {"query_smiles": "Oc1ccccc1",
                                   "target_smiles": "Nc1ccccc1",
                                   "width": 600, "height": 300})
print("depict_mcs:", drawing["status"], drawing["optimal"],
      drawing["matches"][0]["atom_count"], "atoms")
print("svg:", "<svg" in drawing["svg"], drawing["mime_type"],
      drawing["width"], "x", drawing["height"])

# No common graph, no drawing.
none = call_tool("depict_mcs", {"query_smiles": "O", "target_smiles": "N"})
print("no match:", none["found"], none["svg"])

assert not salt["chemical_transformations"] and "." in salt["smiles"]
assert mapped["operations"] == ["remove_atom_maps", "canonical_smiles"]
assert drawing["optimal"] and drawing["matches"][0]["atom_count"] == 6
assert none["svg"] is None

The program prints:

smiles: C(c1ccccc1)([O-])=O.[Na+] | backend: smsd
operations: ['canonical_smiles'] | chemical transformations: False
atom maps removed: CO ['remove_atom_maps', 'canonical_smiles']
depict_mcs: COMPLETED True 6 atoms
svg: True image/svg+xml 600 x 300
no match: False None

cleanup, largest_fragment, neutralise and canonical_tautomer change the chemical graph, so each must be asked for explicitly, and they need the rdkit extra; without it the call raises ImportError, and there is no silent fallback. With any of them set, backend is rdkit, operations lists each step in order and chemical_transformations is true. A canonical tautomer is a choice of representation, not a prediction of the most stable form. Tautomer enumeration stops at 128 tautomers or 256 transformations; when it stops, the result reports LIMIT_REACHED and complete: false, and the choice is made from the tautomers found.

The drawing highlights the mapped atoms and the input bonds between them. For an MCES search, the selected common bonds are those in bond_mapping; the drawing can also highlight other bonds between mapped atoms. A search with no match returns svg: None, and a stopped search keeps its stopped status when drawn. The SVG is checked before it is returned and contains no scripts, external references or document declarations.

docs.title: Tool definitions for a model API
docs.text:
get_tool_definitions(provider) returns the eight tools as a list of dictionaries in one of four shapes. Pass the list to a model API as its tools, then run each tool call the model makes with call_tool and send the result back. No client is created and nothing is sent anywhere:

import json

from smsd.tool_definitions import TOOL_REGISTRY, get_tool_definitions

for provider in ("mcp", "input-schema", "function", "chat-function"):
    first = get_tool_definitions(provider)[0]
    print(f"{provider}:", sorted(first))

schema = TOOL_REGISTRY["find_mcs"].input_schema
print("required:", schema["required"])
print("timeout_ms:", json.dumps(schema["properties"]["timeout_ms"]))
print("objective:", json.dumps(schema["properties"]["objective"]))
print("additionalProperties:", schema["additionalProperties"])
print("tools:", len(TOOL_REGISTRY), "| first:", next(iter(TOOL_REGISTRY)))

assert len(get_tool_definitions()) == 8
assert get_tool_definitions("chat-function")[0]["function"]["strict"] is False

The program prints:

mcp: ['description', 'inputSchema', 'name']
input-schema: ['description', 'input_schema', 'name']
function: ['description', 'name', 'parameters', 'strict', 'type']
chat-function: ['function', 'type']
required: ['query_smiles', 'target_smiles']
timeout_ms: {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 30000, "default": 1000}
objective: {"type": "string", "enum": ["mcis", "mces"], "default": "mcis"}
additionalProperties: False
tools: 8 | first: find_mcs
provider Shape Typical use mcp (default) name, description, inputSchema MCP tool lists input-schema name, description, input_schema APIs that take an input schema per tool function flat: type: "function", name, description, parameters, strict APIs that take flat function definitions chat-function nested: type: "function", function: {name, description, parameters, strict} Chat-completion APIs and most local model runtimes

Every schema sets additionalProperties: false, marks the required arguments, gives each optional argument its default, and bounds every number, text length and list length. The function shapes set strict: false so that a model may leave out optional arguments and the defaults apply. A client that drops schema keywords cannot widen the limits, because call_tool and the server check every argument themselves. The schemas hold single-argument bounds only; combined limits, such as the atoms of a whole screen, are checked when the tool runs.

Which shape each vendor's API expects, the changes some need, and complete loops for several hosted and local models are in Use the tool definitions from Python. Optional LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters, langchain_tools() and llamaindex_tools(), wrap the same callables with the same bounds; see Function definitions and framework adapters.

docs.title: A tool loop with fixed replies
docs.text:
A tool loop sends the conversation and the tool definitions to a model, runs each tool call the model asks for, appends the results and asks again, until the model answers without a tool call. The loop below has that structure, but a small class returns prepared replies in place of a model, so the program runs offline and gives the same output every time. This is also a convenient way to test your own loop before connecting a model. The replies use the chat-function shape: the first asks for one valid call and one with an unknown argument, the second corrects the call after reading the refusal, and the third answers:

import json

from smsd.tool_definitions import call_tool, get_tool_definitions


class FixedReplies:
    """Stands in for a model: returns the next prepared reply on each request."""

    def __init__(self, replies):
        self.replies, self.requests = list(replies), []

    def create(self, messages, tools):
        self.requests.append({"messages": list(messages), "tools": tools})
        return self.replies.pop(0)


def tool_call(call_id, name, arguments):
    return {"id": call_id, "type": "function",
            "function": {"name": name, "arguments": json.dumps(arguments)}}


def run_tool(name, arguments):
    """Run one tool locally; a refusal goes back to the model as text."""
    try:
        return json.dumps(call_tool(name, json.loads(arguments)))
    except (ValueError, ImportError) as error:
        return json.dumps({"error": str(error)})


pair = {"query_smiles": "c1ccccc1O", "target_smiles": "c1ccccc1N"}
model = FixedReplies([
    # Turn 1: one valid call, and one with an argument the tool does not take.
    {"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [
        tool_call("call_1", "find_mcs", pair),
        tool_call("call_2", "find_mcs", {**pair, "timeout": 500})]},
    # Turn 2: the corrected call, after reading the refusal.
    {"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [
        tool_call("call_3", "find_mcs", {**pair, "timeout_ms": 500})]},
    # Turn 3: the answer, which reports the proof flags.
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "The MCS has 6 atoms; COMPLETED, "
     "optimal and complete, so it is proved maximum.", "tool_calls": None},
])

tools = get_tool_definitions("chat-function")
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Find the MCS of phenol and aniline."}]
while True:
    reply = model.create(messages=messages, tools=tools)
    messages.append(reply)
    if not reply["tool_calls"]:
        break
    for call in reply["tool_calls"]:
        text = run_tool(call["function"]["name"], call["function"]["arguments"])
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": text})
        result = json.loads(text)
        print(call["id"], "->", result.get("error") or
              f"status={result['status']} optimal={result['optimal']} "
              f"atoms={result['matches'][0]['atom_count']}")

print("model requests:", len(model.requests))
print("answer:", messages[-1]["content"])

results = [json.loads(m["content"]) for m in messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
assert results[0]["optimal"] and results[0]["matches"][0]["atom_count"] == 6
assert results[1] == {"error": "Unknown tool argument"}
assert results[2]["budget"]["timeout_ms"] == 500
assert model.requests[0]["tools"][0]["function"]["name"] == "find_mcs"

The program prints:

call_1 -> status=COMPLETED optimal=True atoms=6
call_2 -> Unknown tool argument
call_3 -> status=COMPLETED optimal=True atoms=6
model requests: 3
answer: The MCS has 6 atoms; COMPLETED, optimal and complete, so it is proved maximum.

Two points carry over to a loop with a real model. Send every result back in full, including status, optimal and complete, so that the model can say whether its answer is proved; and catch ValueError and ImportError from call_tool and return the message as the tool result, rather than ending the loop, so that the model can correct its call. To replace the fixed replies with a model, replace model.create with the client call of your model API; Connecting AI assistants shows that change for each API. For a fixed sequence of calls with no model at all, see agent_workflow.py, which screens a list, runs an MCS on each hit and draws the best one.

docs.title: Limits and safety
docs.text:
The limits are fixed in the server and apply equally to call_tool. Each result reports them under limits.

Limit Value Applies to Text argument 16,384 characters Every SMILES or SMARTS argument Atoms per molecule 1,024 Searches and fingerprints Atoms per molecule, depiction 256 depict_mcs Atoms per molecule, standardisation 128 standardise_molecule Search time, timeout_ms Default 1,000; at most 30,000; 0 stops at once find_mcs, find_substructure, search_smarts, depict_mcs Search nodes, node_limit Default 100,000; from 1 to 1,000,000 The same four tools Matches or hits returned At most 32 search_smarts, a screen_molecules page Screen targets At most 64 screen_molecules Combined text 65,536 characters The query and targets of screen_molecules Combined atoms 4,096 molecular_similarity, screen_molecules Fingerprint fp_size up to 65,536; radius up to 8; path_length up to 8; at most 2,000,000 estimated path walks The fingerprint tools Drawing 200 to 1,600 by 150 to 1,200 pixels; SVG at most 1 MiB depict_mcs Result 2 MiB as JSON text Every tool

Points to keep in mind when deploying the tools:

  • Local only. The tools read no files, fetch no URLs and contact no network or model service. Molecular arguments are SMILES or SMARTS text, never paths, URLs, expressions or commands. The server has no network listener.
  • Hosted assistants. A hosted assistant sends your prompts, the tool arguments and the results, including any structures, to its provider. Use a model run on your own machine when structures must not leave it.
  • Time budgets cover the search, not the whole call. They start after the input is parsed and the SMARTS compiled; preparation, depiction and serialisation come on top, and standardisation has no time budget. For a hard deadline, apply process or container limits. The container recipe runs the server with no network access, a read-only file system and memory and CPU caps.
  • No zero node limit. A node_limit of 0 is refused rather than read as unlimited.
  • Natural-language requests are not mapped to options. Only the switches in the schema exist; an assistant cannot ask for an option the tools lack.
  • Approval prompts. Keep your client's tool approval prompts on unless you trust every tool it can call.

docs.title: Search tools
docs.text:
find_mcs, depict_mcs, find_substructure and search_smarts share these arguments where they apply:

Argument Type Default Meaning objective string "mcis" mcis maximises common atoms; mces maximises common bonds (find_mcs, depict_mcs) connected boolean true A single connected common graph, or fragments when false (find_mcs, depict_mcs) query_format string "smarts" How query is read: smarts or smiles (find_substructure) induced boolean false Induced matching: unbonded query atoms must map to unbonded target atoms (find_substructure) max_matches integer 16 Embeddings to return, 1 to 32 (search_smarts) timeout_ms integer 1000 Search time limit, 0 to 30,000 ms node_limit integer 100000 Search node limit, 1 to 1,000,000 match_stereo boolean false Match tetrahedral and double-bond stereochemistry complete_rings_only boolean false Matched ring atoms and bonds lie in fully matched rings ring_matches_ring_only boolean false Ring atoms and bonds match only ring atoms and bonds width, height integer 800, 360 Drawing size, 200 to 1,600 and 150 to 1,200 (depict_mcs)

docs.title: Fingerprint tools
docs.text:
molecular_fingerprint, molecular_similarity and screen_molecules share the fingerprint arguments:

Argument Type Default Meaning kind string "ecfp" ecfp (also circular), fcfp, path, torsion or mcs fp_size integer 2048 Fingerprint width, 1 to 65,536 radius integer 2 Radius of ecfp, circular and fcfp, 0 to 8 path_length integer 7 Longest path, in bonds, of path and mcs, 1 to 8 counts boolean false Position and count pairs instead of set bits; not available for mcs metric string "tanimoto" tanimoto, dice or cosine (molecular_similarity) threshold number 0.7 Lowest Tanimoto score kept, 0 to 1, inclusive (screen_molecules) max_hits integer 32 Hits per page, 1 to 32 (screen_molecules) offset integer 0 First hit of the page, 0 to 64 (screen_molecules)

Fingerprints and similarity describes the fingerprint families and coefficients.

docs.title: standardise_molecule
docs.text:
Argument Type Default Meaning remove_atom_maps boolean false Remove atom-map numbers before writing cleanup boolean false RDKit clean-up of the structure largest_fragment boolean false Keep the largest fragment neutralise boolean false Neutralise charges where possible canonical_tautomer boolean false Write the canonical tautomer

The last four need the rdkit extra.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Each call is independent. The tools keep no state between calls, so a query is prepared again on every call; for many searches with one query, use the Python API.
  • screen_molecules fingerprints the query and every target on each call, and so does molecular_similarity for its pair.
  • elapsed_ms and the timings vary from run to run; do not compare them across machines or ask an assistant to.
  • find_mcs returns one common graph. For every optimal mapping, constraints or the common graph of a series, use the Python API in Maximum common substructure.
  • A capped enumeration or a capped screen page is incomplete, not wrong; ask for the next page or a higher cap, up to the limits above.
  • An empty or whitespace-only argument is refused, and so is a threshold that is not a finite number from 0 to 1.

docs.title: Clustering and diversity
docs.text:
Clustering and diverse selection turn a library into something a chemist can review: a set of series, each led by a representative, or a short list of molecules that cover the library's chemistry. SMSD Pro offers three exact tools on a packed fingerprint index: smsd.butina groups rows around cluster centres, smsd.maxmin picks a fixed number of diverse rows, and FingerprintCorpus.top_k_pairs finds the nearest neighbours of every row. This chapter shows which to use for which task, how the threshold, reordering, seed and chunk size behave, what each costs in time and memory, and what runs on a GPU. Every example uses the inline library of Screening a library: 14 benzodiazepines, 7 common drugs and 512 generated trisubstituted benzenes.

All three tools read a FingerprintCorpus, so they need NumPy, from the numpy extra:

python -m pip install "smsd[numpy]==8.1.0"

docs.title: Choose a method
docs.text:
Task Use Returns Comparison work for n rows Extra memory Group a library into series, each with a representative smsd.butina(corpus, threshold) A list of tuples, centre first About n²/2, plus one pass over the library per cluster; reordering=True adds about n² Two arrays of n entries, about 9 bytes per row Pick a fixed number of diverse rows smsd.maxmin(corpus, count, seed=0) A list of rows in the order picked n for each row picked One array of n entries, 8 bytes per row Find the k nearest neighbours of every row, near-duplicates or outliers corpus.top_k_pairs(k, threshold=0.0) Yields (row, neighbour, Tanimoto), at most k per row, best first About n² k entries per row in progress; n × k if every result is kept List every pair above a similarity corpus.threshold_pairs(threshold) Yields (first, second, Tanimoto), each pair once About n²/2 Up to n²/2 pairs if every result is kept

Some guidance on the choice:

  • Use Butina when the question is "which series does this library contain?". The number of clusters follows from the threshold, not from a target count.
  • Use MaxMin when the question is "which N molecules should we buy, test or inspect first?". The count is fixed and the threshold is implicit.
  • Use top_k_pairs to inspect a library before clustering it: identical fingerprints, close analogues and molecules with no near neighbour all show up in its output.
  • Every method compares fingerprints exactly; none samples the library or approximates a score. The work therefore grows with the square of the row count, or with the row count times the number picked for MaxMin, and the results are the same on every run, every chunk size and every backend.

docs.title: Prepare the input
docs.text:
The three tools take an open FingerprintCorpus, built once with FingerprintCorpus.from_smiles or FingerprintCorpus.create, as Packed fingerprint index describes. Four points matter before clustering:

  • The fingerprint decides the answer. A cluster threshold of 0.5 on ECFP4 bits is a different statement from 0.5 on path bits. The index file records the width and row count but not the options, so keep the FingerprintOptions beside it and state them with every result.
  • Rows are numbers. The index stores no names, and every returned row refers to the input order. Keep the identifiers in a list in the same order.
  • Duplicates are counted. Identical fingerprints score 1 with each other, so a series entered many times has many neighbours and tends to supply the first and largest clusters. Remove duplicate structures first if the counts matter; see Prepare the library.
  • Empty fingerprints score 1 with each other. Empty graphs from malformed SD records therefore fall into one cluster, and they score 0 against every other row. Drop graphs with no atoms before building the index.

docs.title: Cluster a library with Butina
docs.text:
smsd.butina(corpus, threshold=0.7) counts, for every row, the other rows whose Tanimoto similarity is at least the threshold. The row with the most neighbours becomes the first centre and takes all its unassigned neighbours as members; the next centre is the unassigned row with the most neighbours, and so on until every row is assigned. Equal counts go to the lower row. The result is a list of tuples, each with its centre first and the other members in row order, and every row appears in exactly one tuple.

A member reaches the threshold with its centre, but not necessarily with the other members of its cluster. A row also joins the first cluster whose centre reaches it, even when a later centre would be closer. The program below clusters the whole library at 0.5 and checks both properties:

import itertools
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import smsd

NAMED = {
    "diazepam": "CN1C(=O)CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "nordazepam": "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2N1",
    "temazepam": "CN1C(=O)C(O)N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "oxazepam": "OC1N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2NC1=O",
    "lorazepam": "OC1N=C(c2ccccc2Cl)c2cc(Cl)ccc2NC1=O",
    "clonazepam": "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2Cl)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc2N1",
    "nitrazepam": "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc2N1",
    "flunitrazepam": "CN1C(=O)CN=C(c2ccccc2F)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc21",
    "bromazepam": "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccn2)c2cc(Br)ccc2N1",
    "tetrazepam": "CN1C(=O)CN=C(C2=CCCCC2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "alprazolam": "Cc1nnc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1)=NC2",
    "triazolam": "Cc1nnc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1Cl)=NC2",
    "midazolam": "Cc1ncc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1F)=NC2",
    "clobazam": "CN1C(=O)CC(=O)N(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "aspirin": "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O",
    "salicylic acid": "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O",
    "paracetamol": "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1",
    "ibuprofen": "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O",
    "naproxen": "COc1ccc2cc(ccc2c1)C(C)C(=O)O",
    "caffeine": "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C",
    "phenol": "Oc1ccccc1",
}
GROUPS = ["C", "CC", "OC", "N", "O", "F", "Cl", "C(=O)O"]
library = list(NAMED.items()) + [
    (f"GEN-{number:03d}", f"c1c({a})cc({b})cc1{c}")
    for number, (a, b, c) in enumerate(itertools.product(GROUPS, repeat=3))
]
names = [name for name, _ in library]
smiles = [text for _, text in library]
assert len(library) == 533

options = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "library.fp"
    with smsd.FingerprintCorpus.from_smiles(path, smiles,
                                            options=options) as corpus:
        clusters = smsd.butina(corpus, threshold=0.5)
        fingerprints = [corpus.fingerprint(row) for row in range(len(corpus))]

# Every row is in exactly one cluster ...
assert sorted(row for cluster in clusters for row in cluster) == list(range(533))
# ... and every member reaches the threshold with its centre.
for centre, *members in clusters:
    for member in members:
        assert smsd.tanimoto_coefficient(fingerprints[centre],
                                         fingerprints[member]) >= 0.5

sizes = [len(cluster) for cluster in clusters]
print("clusters:", len(clusters), "| singletons:", sizes.count(1))
print("first three:", [(names[c[0]], len(c)) for c in clusters[:3]])
print("clusters that hold the named drugs:")
for cluster in clusters:
    if cluster[0] < 21:
        print(f"  {names[cluster[0]]:<15}", [names[row] for row in cluster[1:]])

# Bromazepam reaches 0.5 with nordazepam, but nordazepam was taken first.
nordazepam, bromazepam = names.index("nordazepam"), names.index("bromazepam")
score = smsd.tanimoto_coefficient(fingerprints[nordazepam],
                                  fingerprints[bromazepam])
print(f"nordazepam and bromazepam: {score:.3f}")
assert len(clusters) == 34 and sizes.count(1) == 11
assert (bromazepam,) in clusters and round(score, 3) == 0.519

The program prints:

clusters: 34 | singletons: 11
first three: [('GEN-511', 67), ('GEN-019', 66), ('GEN-087', 42)]
clusters that hold the named drugs:
  diazepam        ['nordazepam', 'temazepam', 'tetrazepam', 'clobazam']
  oxazepam        ['lorazepam']
  nitrazepam      ['clonazepam']
  alprazolam      ['triazolam', 'midazolam']
  bromazepam      []
  flunitrazepam   []
  aspirin         []
  salicylic acid  []
  paracetamol     []
  ibuprofen       []
  naproxen        []
  caffeine        []
  phenol          []
nordazepam and bromazepam: 0.519

The generated benzenes supply the first and largest clusters because each of their 120 distinct structures occurs several times, so each has many identical neighbours. Bromazepam shows the order effect: it reaches the threshold with nordazepam, but nordazepam had already joined diazepam's cluster, so bromazepam forms a cluster of its own.

docs.title: Thresholds and reordering
docs.text:
The threshold is a Tanimoto similarity, inclusive, from 0 to 1; a higher threshold gives more, tighter clusters. With the default reordering=False the neighbour counts are computed once, before any cluster is taken, so a later centre may be chosen for neighbours that earlier clusters have already claimed. reordering=True recounts after each cluster so that only unassigned neighbours count, and later centres are chosen by the neighbours still available. It costs up to about three times the comparisons. Neither mode is more exact than the other; they answer slightly different questions, so record which one a result used.

import itertools
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import smsd

NAMED = {
    "diazepam": "CN1C(=O)CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "nordazepam": "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2N1",
    "temazepam": "CN1C(=O)C(O)N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21",
    "oxazepam": "OC1N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2NC1=O",
