docs.title: Machine learning and data frames
docs.text: The smsd.adapters module turns SMSD Pro fingerprints into the structures that data and machine-learning libraries expect: NumPy matrices, SciPy sparse matrices, pandas and Polars columns, Arrow tables, PyTorch tensors and scikit-learn transformers. This chapter shows which adapter suits which data stack, how each one is used, and the points about data types, bit order, copies and memory that decide whether a pipeline is correct and affordable. A worked example at the end fingerprints a small set of molecules, trains two scikit-learn models in pipelines and screens the same molecules by similarity.

docs.title: Choose an adapter
docs.text:
Data stack Use Returns Extra NumPy arrays fingerprints_numpy, or to_numpy on fingerprints already computed A dense matrix, one row per molecule; uint8 bits or int64 counts numpy SciPy sparse matrices fingerprints_scipy, or to_scipy A CSR matrix with sorted columns; uint8 bits or int64 counts scipy pandas molecules_pandas A data frame with molecule and fingerprint object columns pandas Polars molecules_polars A data frame with an Object molecule column and a typed list fingerprint column polars Arrow, and tools that read Arrow to_arrow on a NumPy matrix A table with one fixed-size-list fingerprint column, shared with the matrix where possible arrow scikit-learn, fingerprint features FingerprintTransformer A transformer whose output is the fingerprints_numpy matrix sklearn scikit-learn, similarity features or a Tanimoto kernel SimilarityTransformer A transformer whose output is a float64 Tanimoto matrix against fitted references sklearn PyTorch fingerprints_torch, or to_torch A tensor, on the CPU unless a device is given torch PyTorch Geometric to_pyg A Data object with atom and bond features of one molecule pyg

As a rule of thumb, take a dense NumPy matrix when the model needs one and the library fits in memory, a CSR matrix when it does not and the estimator accepts sparse input, and the data-frame adapters when molecules and fingerprints must stay next to other columns. Arrow is for handing fingerprints to another process or file format without a copy. For library-scale similarity searching, a packed fingerprint index is better suited than a feature matrix.

Install the extras that the chosen adapters need, for example python -m pip install "smsd[sklearn,pandas,arrow]==8.1.0"; Getting started lists every extra. Importing smsd.adapters loads none of these packages; each function loads its own when it is called and raises ImportError naming the extra when the package is missing.

docs.title: Feature matrices with NumPy
docs.text:
fingerprints_numpy(molecules, ...) computes the fingerprints and expands them to a matrix in one call. Column j is fingerprint position j. Bits are uint8 and counts are int64 unless dtype says otherwise. to_numpy does the same for sparse fingerprints that have already been computed, such as the output of smsd.fingerprints. Both accept SMILES strings, MolGraph objects and RDKit molecules.

import numpy as np
import smsd
from smsd.adapters import fingerprints_numpy, to_numpy

smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O", "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1",
          "Oc1ccccc1"]  # aspirin, salicylic acid, paracetamol, phenol
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)

# One row per molecule, one column per bit position.
bits = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, options=ecfp4)
print("bits:", bits.shape, bits.dtype, f"{bits.nbytes:,} bytes")
print("set bits per row:", bits.sum(axis=1).tolist())
assert bits.dtype == np.uint8 and bits.sum(axis=1).tolist() == [36, 28, 24, 14]

# The same matrix from sparse positions computed earlier.
positions = smsd.fingerprints(smiles, options=ecfp4)
assert (to_numpy(positions, fp_size=2048) == bits).all()
assert bits[0].nonzero()[0].tolist() == positions[0]

# Count fingerprints: one column per bin, int64 counts.
counts_options = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)
counts_options.counts = True
counts = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, options=counts_options)
print("counts:", counts.shape, counts.dtype, f"{counts.nbytes:,} bytes")
print("largest count per row:", counts.max(axis=1).tolist())
assert counts.dtype == np.int64 and counts.max(axis=1).tolist() == [3, 3, 4, 4]
assert ((counts > 0) == (bits > 0)).all()

# Without kind or options the family is "mcs", not ECFP.
default = fingerprints_numpy(smiles)
print("default kind equals ECFP4:", bool((default == bits).all()))
assert not (default == bits).all()

The program prints:

bits: (4, 2048) uint8 8,192 bytes
set bits per row: [36, 28, 24, 14]
counts: (4, 2048) int64 65,536 bytes
largest count per row: [3, 3, 4, 4]
default kind equals ECFP4: False

Like smsd.fingerprints, fingerprints_numpy defaults to kind="mcs"; pass kind or options every time. When options is given, its size and counts decide the width and the data type of the matrix. A count matrix is eight times the size of a bit matrix of the same width. NumPy arrays in the fingerprint chapter shows a Tanimoto matrix computed from such a matrix with one product.

docs.title: Sparse matrices with SciPy
docs.text:
A 2,048-bit ECFP4 row of a drug-like molecule has a few dozen set bits, so most of a dense matrix is zeros. fingerprints_scipy and to_scipy return a SciPy CSR matrix without ever building the dense matrix. Only integer and boolean data types are accepted.

import itertools

import smsd
from smsd.adapters import fingerprints_numpy, fingerprints_scipy

GROUPS = ["C", "CC", "OC", "N", "O", "F", "Cl", "C(=O)O"]
smiles = [f"c1c({a})cc({b})cc1{c}"
          for a, b, c in itertools.product(GROUPS, repeat=3)]
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)

dense = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, options=ecfp4)
sparse = fingerprints_scipy(smiles, options=ecfp4)
sparse_bytes = sparse.data.nbytes + sparse.indices.nbytes + sparse.indptr.nbytes
density = sparse.nnz / (sparse.shape[0] * sparse.shape[1])
print("molecules:", sparse.shape[0], "| set bits:", sparse.nnz,
      f"| density: {density:.4f}")
print(f"dense: {dense.nbytes:,} bytes | CSR: {sparse_bytes:,} bytes")
assert (sparse.toarray() == dense).all() and sparse.dtype == dense.dtype
assert sparse.nnz == 12874

The program prints:

molecules: 512 | set bits: 12874 | density: 0.0123
dense: 1,048,576 bytes | CSR: 66,422 bytes

The CSR matrix stores each set bit as a value and a 64-bit column index, so for uint8 bits it saves memory only while fewer than about one position in nine is set. Most scikit-learn linear models and nearest-neighbour estimators accept CSR input; check the estimator before relying on it, because one that needs dense input will convert the whole matrix.

docs.title: pandas and Polars columns
docs.text:
molecules_pandas and molecules_polars return a data frame with two columns, in input order: molecule, holding the parsed MolGraph, and fingerprint, holding the sorted set-bit positions. Further columns, such as names or measured values, are added in the usual way. to_numpy turns the fingerprint column into a feature matrix when a model needs one.

import polars as pl
import smsd
from smsd.adapters import molecules_pandas, molecules_polars, to_numpy

names = ["aspirin", "salicylic acid", "paracetamol", "phenol"]
smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O", "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1",
          "Oc1ccccc1"]
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)

# pandas: object columns, one MolGraph and one tuple of positions per row.
frame = molecules_pandas(smiles, options=ecfp4)
frame.insert(0, "name", names)
frame["atoms"] = [graph.n for graph in frame["molecule"]]
frame["bits"] = frame["fingerprint"].map(len)
print(frame[["name", "atoms", "bits"]].to_string(index=False))
print("pandas columns:", frame["molecule"].dtype, frame["fingerprint"].dtype)
X = to_numpy(frame["fingerprint"], fp_size=2048)
print("pandas features:", X.shape, X.dtype)

# Polars: an Object column for molecules and a typed list of positions.
table = molecules_polars(smiles, options=ecfp4).with_columns(
    pl.Series("name", names),
    pl.col("fingerprint").list.len().alias("bits"),
)
print("polars columns:", table.schema["molecule"], table.schema["fingerprint"])
Y = to_numpy(table["fingerprint"].to_list(), fp_size=2048)
assert (X == Y).all()
assert table["bits"].to_list() == frame["bits"].tolist() == [36, 28, 24, 14]
assert isinstance(frame["molecule"].iloc[0], smsd.MolGraph)

The program prints:

          name  atoms  bits
       aspirin     13    36
salicylic acid     10    28
   paracetamol     11    24
        phenol      7    14
pandas columns: object object
pandas features: (4, 2048) uint8
polars columns: Object List(UInt64)

pandas stores the fingerprints as immutable tuples; Polars stores them as lists of uint64 positions, or lists of [position, count] pairs with count options. Both functions accept only MolGraph objects and SMILES strings, and raise TypeError for anything else, including RDKit molecules and missing values; convert or drop those rows first. The frames hold references to the molecules rather than copies.

A Polars Object column cannot be exported to Arrow. Drop the molecule column, or keep the SMILES in a string column, before writing a Polars frame to Parquet or Arrow.

docs.title: Arrow tables and zero-copy export
docs.text:
to_arrow writes one fingerprint column as an Arrow fixed-size list of integers. When it is given a two-dimensional, C-contiguous, native-endian integer NumPy matrix, the Arrow column uses the matrix's memory directly, and Arrow keeps the matrix alive for as long as the table exists. Other boolean or integer input is copied once into a new matrix first, and floating-point input is rejected. The schema metadata says which happened, and zero_copy_only=True turns a needed copy into a ValueError.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import smsd
from smsd.adapters import fingerprints_numpy, to_arrow

smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O", "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1",
          "Oc1ccccc1"]
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)
bits = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, options=ecfp4)


def report(label, table):
    metadata = table.schema.metadata
    print(f"{label:18} zero copy {metadata[b'smsd.zero_copy'].decode():5}  "
          f"reason {metadata[b'smsd.copy_reason'].decode()}")
    return metadata[b"smsd.zero_copy"] == b"true"


# A C-contiguous integer matrix shares its buffer with the Arrow column.
shared = to_arrow(bits, fp_size=2048, zero_copy_only=True)
print("type:", shared.schema.field("fingerprint").type)
assert report("uint8 matrix", shared)
values = shared.column("fingerprint").chunk(0).values
assert np.shares_memory(values.to_numpy(zero_copy_only=True), bits)

# These inputs need a copy, and the metadata says why.
assert not report("boolean matrix", to_arrow(bits.astype(bool), fp_size=2048))
assert not report("column slice", to_arrow(bits[:, :1024], fp_size=1024))
positions = smsd.fingerprints(smiles, options=ecfp4)
assert not report("sparse positions", to_arrow(positions, fp_size=2048))
assert not report("copy=True", to_arrow(bits, fp_size=2048, copy=True))
try:
    to_arrow(bits.astype(bool), fp_size=2048, zero_copy_only=True)
except ValueError as error:
    print("zero_copy_only:", error)

# Polars reads the table as a fixed-width array column.
frame = pl.from_arrow(shared)
print("polars:", frame.schema["fingerprint"],
      frame["fingerprint"].to_numpy().shape)

# Shared values alias the source: a change to the matrix shows in the table.
assert bits[3, 0] == 0
bits[3, 0] = 1
seen = shared.column("fingerprint")[3].values[0].as_py()
print("table sees the change:", seen)
assert seen == 1

The program prints:

type: fixed_size_list<item: uint8>[2048]
uint8 matrix       zero copy true   reason none
boolean matrix     zero copy false  reason layout_or_boolean
column slice       zero copy false  reason layout_or_boolean
sparse positions   zero copy false  reason sparse_expansion
copy=True          zero copy false  reason requested
zero_copy_only: This dtype or layout requires a copy
polars: Array(UInt8, shape=(2048,)) (4, 2048)
table sees the change: 1

The rules for a copy-free export:

  • Use an integer data type. A boolean matrix is converted to uint8, because Arrow packs booleans as bits; a floating-point matrix is rejected, also in count mode.
  • Keep the matrix C-contiguous. A column slice, a transposed matrix or a Fortran-ordered matrix is copied, as is a stepped slice of rows such as bits[::2]; a contiguous range of whole rows is not.
  • Keep the byte order native. A big-endian matrix on a little-endian machine is copied.
  • Do not change the matrix while the table is in use, as the last lines of the program show. Pass copy=True when the table must be independent of it.

copy=True and zero_copy_only=True cannot be combined. The dtype argument applies only when sparse positions are expanded; passing it with a NumPy matrix raises ValueError. The table carries fingerprint features only, not the molecules, and the export is a memory operation, not a transfer to a GPU.

docs.title: Packed bytes and bit order
docs.text:
A packed fingerprint index stores bit p of a row in byte p // 8, at bit p % 8: bit 0 is the least significant bit of the first byte. NumPy's packbits and unpackbits use the opposite order unless they are told otherwise, so pass bitorder="little" whenever packed bytes are exchanged with an index:

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import smsd
from smsd.adapters import fingerprints_numpy

smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "Oc1ccccc1"]  # aspirin, phenol
bits = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2)

little = np.packbits(bits, axis=1, bitorder="little")
big = np.packbits(bits, axis=1)  # NumPy's default is bitorder="big"
print("packed:", little.shape, little.dtype)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "two.smsdfp"
    with smsd.FingerprintCorpus.from_smiles(path, smiles, kind="ecfp",
                                            fp_size=2048, radius=2) as index:
        (start, stored), = index.iter_packed_chunks()
        print("matches bitorder='little':", bool((stored == little).all()))
        print("matches the default order:", bool((stored == big).all()))
        assert (stored == little).all() and not (stored == big).all()
        assert (np.unpackbits(stored, axis=1, bitorder="little") == bits).all()

The program prints:

packed: (2, 256) uint8
matches bitorder='little': True
matches the default order: False

A wrong bit order raises no error: the bytes are valid, but every similarity computed from them is wrong. The matrices of smsd.adapters hold one column per position and have no bit order to get wrong.

docs.title: scikit-learn transformers
docs.text:
FingerprintTransformer wraps fingerprints_numpy as a scikit-learn transformer. It takes a one-dimensional sequence of molecules (a list, a pandas Series or one column selected by a ColumnTransformer) and returns the feature matrix. It learns nothing: fit only marks it fitted, so the same molecules always give the same features, inside or outside cross-validation. Its parameters are ordinary estimator parameters and work with clone, set_params and grid searches.

SimilarityTransformer stores the binary fingerprints of the molecules passed to fit, in order and with duplicates, and transform returns one float64 column per stored reference: the Tanimoto similarity of each input molecule to that reference.

import pandas as pd
import smsd
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from smsd.adapters import FingerprintTransformer, SimilarityTransformer

smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O",
          "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1",
          "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1", "Oc1ccccc1", "Clc1ccccc1",
          "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C"]
data = pd.DataFrame({
    "smiles": smiles,
    "heavy_atoms": [smsd.parse_smiles(text).n for text in smiles],
    "acid": [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0],  # 1: carboxylic acid
})

# A transformer on its own: fit records nothing, transform fingerprints.
fingerprint = FingerprintTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=1024)
X = fingerprint.fit_transform(data["smiles"])
print("features:", X.shape, X.dtype, "| first names:",
      fingerprint.get_feature_names_out()[:3].tolist())

# A column of SMILES beside a numeric column, in one pipeline.
features = ColumnTransformer([
    ("fingerprint", FingerprintTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=1024),
     "smiles"),
    ("size", "passthrough", ["heavy_atoms"]),
])
model = make_pipeline(features, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
model.fit(data[["smiles", "heavy_atoms"]], data["acid"])
predictions = model.predict(data[["smiles", "heavy_atoms"]]).tolist()
print("predictions:", predictions)
assert predictions == data["acid"].tolist()

# Parameters work with clone and set_params, as for any estimator.
wider = clone(model).set_params(columntransformer__fingerprint__fp_size=2048)
wider.fit(data[["smiles", "heavy_atoms"]], data["acid"])
print("model inputs after widening:", wider[-1].n_features_in_)
assert wider[-1].n_features_in_ == 2049

# Tanimoto similarity to fitted references, one column per reference.
references = SimilarityTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048).fit(smiles[:2])
scores = references.transform(["OC(=O)c1ccccc1"]).round(3).tolist()
print("columns:", references.get_feature_names_out().tolist())
print("benzoic acid:", scores)
assert scores == [[0.256, 0.278]]
references.set_params(fp_size=1024)
try:
    references.transform(["OC(=O)c1ccccc1"])
except ValueError as error:
    print("after set_params:", error)

The program prints:

features: (8, 1024) uint8 | first names: ['fp_0', 'fp_1', 'fp_2']
predictions: [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
model inputs after widening: 2049
columns: ['reference_0', 'reference_1']
benzoic acid: [[0.256, 0.278]]
after set_params: Fingerprint parameters changed; refit SimilarityTransformer

The training predictions only show that the pipeline runs; they are not a measure of model quality.

Transformer Learns in fit Output Output size Molecule input FingerprintTransformer Nothing uint8 bits, int64 counts or the chosen dtype Molecules times fp_size SMILES, MolGraph or RDKit molecules SimilarityTransformer The reference fingerprints float64 Tanimoto values Molecules times references SMILES or MolGraph only

Choose FingerprintTransformer when the model should weigh individual structural features, as linear models, tree ensembles and neural networks do. Choose SimilarityTransformer when similarity to known molecules is the signal: as the features of a nearest-neighbour model, as a precomputed kernel (see the worked example), or as a column of "distance to the nearest active" beside other descriptors.

docs.title: PyTorch tensors
docs.text:
fingerprints_torch and to_torch return a tensor of the same shape and with the same default types as the NumPy adapters, without needing NumPy. The tensor is created on the CPU unless device names another device, and its type follows dtype. Write the call so that a missing or unusable PyTorch is handled:

import smsd
from smsd.adapters import fingerprints_numpy, fingerprints_torch

smiles = ["CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O", "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1",
          "Oc1ccccc1"]
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)

try:
    # The adapter checks the runtime before it imports PyTorch.
    features = fingerprints_torch(smiles, options=ecfp4)
except ImportError as error:
    print("PyTorch features unavailable:", error)
    features = fingerprints_numpy(smiles, options=ecfp4)
    print("NumPy features instead:", features.shape, features.dtype)
else:
    import torch  # already loaded by the adapter

    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        features = features.to(device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    print("tensor:", tuple(features.shape), features.dtype, features.device)
assert tuple(features.shape) == (4, 2048)

Without PyTorch, the program prints:

PyTorch features unavailable: This adapter requires torch; install smsd[torch]
NumPy features instead: (4, 2048) uint8

With PyTorch installed, the program prints one tensor: line instead: a torch.uint8 tensor on the CPU, or, where PyTorch reports a usable CUDA device, a torch.float32 tensor on that device. Fingerprints are always computed on CPU threads; the device argument and .to() move only the finished tensor. On macOS, a packaged SMSD wheel built with OpenMP and PyTorch can load two different OpenMP runtimes, which can stop the process. The adapters detect this before importing PyTorch and raise ImportError, which the program above catches; the remedy is an SMSD build without OpenMP, or packages linked to one shared OpenMP runtime, as described in NumPy and PyTorch. Call the adapter before importing PyTorch yourself, so that the check runs first.

to_pyg turns one molecule into a PyTorch Geometric Data object with seven integer atom features and three integer bond features per directed edge; PyTorch Geometric molecular graphs lists them.

docs.title: A worked example: train and screen
docs.text:
This program uses 18 labelled molecules to train two models, one on fingerprint features and one on Tanimoto similarity as a kernel, and scores 8 held-out molecules with both. It then screens the same held-out molecules by their highest similarity to the known actives, and prints the three views side by side. The label marks the benzodiazepines; it is illustrative, and a set of this size says nothing about predictive performance.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from smsd.adapters import FingerprintTransformer, SimilarityTransformer

# Training set: label 1 for a benzodiazepine, 0 otherwise.
TRAIN = [
    ("diazepam", "CN1C(=O)CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21", 1),
    ("nordazepam", "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2N1", 1),
    ("temazepam", "CN1C(=O)C(O)N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21", 1),
    ("oxazepam", "OC1N=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc(Cl)ccc2NC1=O", 1),
    ("lorazepam", "OC1N=C(c2ccccc2Cl)c2cc(Cl)ccc2NC1=O", 1),
    ("clonazepam", "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2Cl)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc2N1", 1),
    ("nitrazepam", "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccc2)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc2N1", 1),
    ("alprazolam", "Cc1nnc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1)=NC2", 1),
    ("triazolam", "Cc1nnc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1Cl)=NC2", 1),
    ("aspirin", "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O", 0),
    ("salicylic acid", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1O", 0),
    ("ibuprofen", "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O", 0),
    ("naproxen", "COc1ccc2cc(ccc2c1)C(C)C(=O)O", 0),
    ("caffeine", "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C", 0),
    ("phenol", "Oc1ccccc1", 0),
    ("benzophenone", "O=C(c1ccccc1)c1ccccc1", 0),
    ("4-chloroaniline", "Nc1ccc(Cl)cc1", 0),
    ("acetanilide", "CC(=O)Nc1ccccc1", 0),
]
# Held-out molecules, scored after training.
TEST = [
    ("flunitrazepam", "CN1C(=O)CN=C(c2ccccc2F)c2cc([N+](=O)[O-])ccc21", 1),
    ("bromazepam", "O=C1CN=C(c2ccccn2)c2cc(Br)ccc2N1", 1),
    ("midazolam", "Cc1ncc2n1-c1ccc(Cl)cc1C(c1ccccc1F)=NC2", 1),
    ("tetrazepam", "CN1C(=O)CN=C(C2=CCCCC2)c2cc(Cl)ccc21", 1),
    ("paracetamol", "CC(=O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1", 0),
    ("2-aminobenzophenone", "Nc1ccccc1C(=O)c1ccccc1", 0),
    ("chlorobenzene", "Clc1ccccc1", 0),
    ("benzoic acid", "OC(=O)c1ccccc1", 0),
]
train_smiles = [smiles for _, smiles, _ in TRAIN]
y_train = np.array([label for _, _, label in TRAIN])
test_names = [name for name, _, _ in TEST]
test_smiles = [smiles for _, smiles, _ in TEST]
y_test = np.array([label for _, _, label in TEST])

# 1. Fingerprint features and a linear model.
linear = make_pipeline(
    FingerprintTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2),
    LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000),
)
linear.fit(train_smiles, y_train)
probability = linear.predict_proba(test_smiles)[:, 1]

# 2. A Tanimoto kernel: the similarity matrix to the training molecules is
#    the precomputed kernel of a support vector machine.
kernel = make_pipeline(
    SimilarityTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2),
    SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=1.0),
)
kernel.fit(train_smiles, y_train)
margin = kernel.decision_function(test_smiles)

# 3. A similarity screen: the nearest known active for each test molecule.
active_names = [name for name, _, label in TRAIN if label == 1]
actives = [smiles for _, smiles, label in TRAIN if label == 1]
screen = SimilarityTransformer(kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2).fit(actives)
scores = screen.transform(test_smiles)
best = scores.max(axis=1)
nearest = scores.argmax(axis=1)

print(f"{'molecule':20} {'label':>5} {'P(active)':>9} {'margin':>7} "
      f"{'Tanimoto':>8}  nearest active")
order = np.argsort(-best, kind="stable")
for i in order:
    print(f"{test_names[i]:20} {y_test[i]:5d} {probability[i]:9.3f} "
          f"{margin[i]:7.3f} {best[i]:8.3f}  {active_names[nearest[i]]}")
hits = [test_names[i] for i in order if best[i] >= 0.4]
for label, model in (("linear", linear), ("kernel", kernel)):
    correct = int((model.predict(test_smiles) == y_test).sum())
    print(f"{label} model correct: {correct} of 8")
print("screen hits at Tanimoto >= 0.4:", hits)

assert ((probability > 0.5) == (y_test == 1)).all()
assert ((margin > 0) == (y_test == 1)).all()
assert best.round(3).tolist() == [0.465, 0.519, 0.541, 0.542, 0.031, 0.125,
                                  0.256, 0.154]
assert hits == ["tetrazepam", "midazolam", "bromazepam", "flunitrazepam"]

The program prints:

molecule             label P(active)  margin Tanimoto  nearest active
tetrazepam               1     0.792   0.320    0.542  diazepam
midazolam                1     0.860   0.444    0.541  triazolam
bromazepam               1     0.841   0.387    0.519  nordazepam
flunitrazepam            1     0.835   0.424    0.465  clonazepam
chlorobenzene            0     0.181  -0.436    0.256  diazepam
benzoic acid             0     0.069  -0.730    0.154  oxazepam
2-aminobenzophenone      0     0.056  -0.735    0.125  nordazepam
paracetamol              0     0.031  -0.698    0.031  diazepam
linear model correct: 8 of 8
kernel model correct: 8 of 8
screen hits at Tanimoto >= 0.4: ['tetrazepam', 'midazolam', 'bromazepam', 'flunitrazepam']

The three columns answer different questions. The probability and the margin come from models that weigh the training molecules of both classes; the Tanimoto column depends only on the actives and is the easiest to explain, since the nearest active can be shown beside each hit. The Tanimoto values are exact for the chosen fingerprint. The probabilities and margins come from numerical solvers and may differ in the last digit between platforms or library versions.

The kernel pipeline is correct as written because SimilarityTransformer returns the training molecules against themselves when the pipeline is fitted, and new molecules against the training molecules when it predicts, which are the two matrices a precomputed kernel needs. It holds one float64 value per pair, so it suits training sets of thousands of molecules, not millions.

To take the hits further, confirm the shared scaffold with an exact search, as in Screening a library. For a library too large to hold as a feature matrix, screen it with TargetCorpus or a streamed screen, or with a packed fingerprint index, and pass only the shortlist to the model.

docs.title: Feature functions
docs.text:
Function Fingerprint arguments Other arguments Returns fingerprints_numpy(molecules, ...) kind="mcs", path_length=7, fp_size=2048, radius=2, options=None num_threads=0, dtype=None NumPy matrix fingerprints_scipy(molecules, ...) kind="ecfp", path_length=7, fp_size=2048, radius=2, options=None num_threads=0, dtype=None SciPy CSR matrix fingerprints_torch(molecules, ...) kind="mcs", path_length=7, fp_size=2048, radius=2, options=None num_threads=0, dtype=None, device="cpu" PyTorch tensor molecules_pandas(molecules, ...) kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2, path_length=7, options=None num_threads=0 pandas data frame molecules_polars(molecules, ...) kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2, path_length=7, options=None num_threads=0 Polars data frame

All arguments after molecules are keywords. The fingerprint arguments mean what they mean for smsd.fingerprints, and options, when given, sets the fingerprint completely, including its width and count mode. num_threads=0 uses the OpenMP default. A single SMILES string passed as molecules raises TypeError; wrap it in a list.

docs.title: Conversion functions
docs.text:
Function Arguments Returns to_numpy(sparse_fingerprints, *, fp_size=2048, counts=False, dtype=None) Positions, or (position, count) pairs when counts=True NumPy matrix; boolean, integer or floating-point dtype to_scipy(sparse_fingerprints, *, fp_size=2048, counts=False, dtype=None) As to_numpy CSR matrix; boolean or integer dtype to_torch(sparse_fingerprints, *, fp_size=2048, counts=False, dtype=None, device="cpu") As to_numpy Tensor; a torch.dtype to_arrow(fingerprints, *, fp_size=2048, counts=False, dtype=None, copy=False, zero_copy_only=False) A NumPy matrix of width fp_size, or sparse rows Arrow table with schema metadata to_pyg(molecule, *, device="cpu") One SMILES string or MolGraph PyTorch Geometric Data

The conversion functions read sparse rows only. A dense row of zeros and ones passed to to_numpy, to_scipy or to_torch raises no error: it is read as positions, so [[0, 1, 0, 1]] becomes bits 0 and 1. Positions outside fp_size, negative counts and counts that do not fit the chosen type raise ValueError; repeated count bins are added together. An empty batch gives shape (0, fp_size).

docs.title: Arrow schema metadata
docs.text: Key Values Meaning smsd.fp_size The width Fingerprint width in bits or bins smsd.counts true, false Whether the values are counts smsd.zero_copy true, false Whether the column shares the caller's matrix smsd.copy_reason none, layout_or_boolean, sparse_expansion, requested Why a copy was made smsd.ownership shared_numpy_owner_retained, owned_numpy_owner_retained Whose matrix the table keeps alive

docs.title: Transformers
docs.text:
Transformer Parameters, with defaults Fitted attributes FingerprintTransformer kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2, path_length=7, counts=False, dtype=None, num_threads=0 is_fitted_ SimilarityTransformer kind="ecfp", fp_size=2048, radius=2, path_length=7, num_threads=0 reference_fingerprints_, n_references_

Both are keyword-only and both name their output columns through get_feature_names_out(): fp_0, fp_1 and so on, or reference_0, reference_1 and so on. FingerprintTransformer(counts=True) supports the ECFP, FCFP, path and torsion families. SimilarityTransformer always uses binary fingerprints, raises ValueError when fitted with no references, and gives a similarity of 1 between two empty fingerprints.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Fingerprint family. fingerprints_numpy and fingerprints_torch default to kind="mcs", while fingerprints_scipy, the data-frame adapters and both transformers default to kind="ecfp". Pass the kind or a FingerprintOptions everywhere, so that training features and screening features come from the same fingerprint.
  • One molecule. A bare SMILES string raises TypeError rather than being read character by character; pass ["CCO"], not "CCO".
  • Input types. molecules_pandas, molecules_polars, SimilarityTransformer and to_pyg accept only SMILES strings and MolGraph objects. Missing values in a SMILES column raise TypeError; drop or fill them first.
  • Data types. Bits arrive as uint8 and counts as int64. An estimator that works in float64 converts the matrix, which makes a copy eight times the size of the uint8 matrix. Choose dtype once, at the adapter, rather than converting large matrices repeatedly. A floating-point dtype can lose precision for very large counts.
  • Memory. A dense 2,048-bit matrix needs 2,048 bytes per molecule as uint8 and 16,384 bytes as int64 or float64: about 2 GB and 16 GB for a million molecules. Use fingerprints_scipy, smaller chunks or a packed fingerprint index beyond that. The output of SimilarityTransformer grows with queries times references.
  • Copies. Arrow shares only C-contiguous, native-endian integer matrices. Slicing columns, transposing or converting to boolean before to_arrow forces a copy. A shared table changes when its matrix changes.
  • Bit order. Matrices hold one column per position. Packed bytes in an index are little-endian within each byte, unlike NumPy's default packbits order.
  • Width. Positions are hashed into fp_size columns, so different structures can share a column. A width that is too narrow for the molecules saturates the fingerprint; fingerprint quality shows how to check.
  • Refitting. Changing a SimilarityTransformer parameter after fit makes transform raise until it is fitted again. FingerprintTransformer reads its parameters at every transform.
  • Feature names in a ColumnTransformer. A FingerprintTransformer inside a ColumnTransformer fits and transforms normally, but the ColumnTransformer's get_feature_names_out() raises ValueError, because the transformer refuses input column names. Call get_feature_names_out() on the fingerprint transformer itself.
  • Devices. A device argument places the finished tensor. Fingerprints and graph features are always computed on the CPU, and smsd-cuda plays no part in these adapters; see What runs where.

docs.title: Maximum common substructure
docs.text: A maximum common substructure (MCS) search finds the largest graph that two molecules share under a set of chemistry rules. SMSD Pro offers two objectives: the maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS), which maximises common atoms, and the maximum common edge subgraph (MCES), which maximises common bonds. Either can be connected or split into fragments. Every result states whether it is proved optimal, so a stopped search never passes for a complete one. This chapter covers the objectives, limits and partial results, chemistry options, atom weights, reserved atoms, common graphs of a series, validation, MCS similarity, export, drawing and tautomers.

docs.title: Prepare and run a search
docs.text:
smsd.MCS.find(query) prepares a query once from a SMILES string, a MolGraph or an RDKit molecule. The prepared query is immutable and can be shared between threads; with_timeout, with_options, with_objective, with_fragments and with_atom_weights each return a new query and leave the original unchanged. match(target) returns a SearchResult with at most one Match.

import smsd

query, target = "c1ccc(O)cc1", "c1ccc(N)cc1"  # phenol, aniline
prepared = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(1000)
result = prepared.match(target)
best = result.best

assert result.found and result.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED
assert result.optimal and result.complete and result.score == 6.0
assert (best.atom_count, best.bond_count) == (6, 6)
mapping = sorted(best.atom_mapping.items())
assert mapping == [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (5, 5), (6, 6)]
assert best.bond_mapping[0] == (0, 1, 0, 1) and len(best.bond_mapping) == 6
assert best.fragments == ((0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6),)
assert best.to_smiles(query) == "c1ccccc1"

print("status:", result.status.name, "| optimal:", result.optimal,
      "| complete:", result.complete)
print("score:", result.score, "| atoms:", best.atom_count,
      "| bonds:", best.bond_count)
print("atom mapping:", mapping)
print("first bond:", best.bond_mapping[0], "of", len(best.bond_mapping))
print("fragments:", best.fragments)
print("common graph:", best.to_smiles(query))

The program prints:

status: COMPLETED | optimal: True | complete: True
score: 6.0 | atoms: 6 | bonds: 6
atom mapping: [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (5, 5), (6, 6)]
first bond: (0, 1, 0, 1) of 6
fragments: ((0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6),)
common graph: c1ccccc1

The result fields are:

Field Meaning found, best, matches Whether a match exists; the first Match or None; all matches as a tuple status COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED or LIMIT_REACHED optimal The optimum is proved complete The search, or the enumeration of match_all, finished score Atoms for MCIS, bonds for MCES, weight units with atom weights nodes_visited, elapsed_ms Search effort and elapsed milliseconds, for diagnostics only

Each Match holds atom_mapping (a read-only map from query atom to target atom), bond_mapping (one (query_first, query_second, target_first, target_second) tuple per selected bond), fragments (the components of the common graph, as query atom indices), atom_count and bond_count. Indices follow the caller's numbering, including the atom order of an RDKit molecule. The mapping of an RDKit input is not sorted by key, so sort it before printing. Reading a result explains the three status fields in more depth.

docs.title: MCIS and MCES
docs.text:
MCIS, the default, ranks common graphs by atoms and then by bonds. The mapped atoms keep every bond and every non-bond between them, so the common graph is an induced subgraph of both molecules. MCES ranks by bonds and then by atoms. It may leave out a bond between two mapped atoms, and it never keeps an atom without a selected bond.

import smsd

query, target = "C1CC1", "CC(C)C"  # cyclopropane, isobutane
induced = smsd.MCS.find(query).match(target)
edges = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_objective(smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES).match(target)

rows = []
for label, result in (("MCIS", induced), ("MCES", edges)):
    assert result.optimal
    best = result.best
    rows.append((label, best.atom_count, best.bond_count, result.score,
                 best.to_smiles(query)))
assert rows == [("MCIS", 2, 1, 2.0, "CC"), ("MCES", 3, 2, 2.0, "C(C)C")]
for label, atoms, bonds, score, smiles in rows:
    print(f"{label}: atoms {atoms}, bonds {bonds}, score {score}, {smiles}")

The program prints:

MCIS: atoms 2, bonds 1, score 2.0, CC
MCES: atoms 3, bonds 2, score 2.0, C(C)C

Both scores are 2.0, but they count different things: two atoms for MCIS and two bonds for MCES. Compare scores only between searches with the same objective.

docs.title: Connected or fragments
docs.text:
By default the common graph is connected. with_fragments(min_atoms=1, max_fragments=2147483647) allows several components, each of at least min_atoms atoms, up to max_fragments components. With min_atoms=1, MCIS can keep isolated atoms; MCES never does.

import smsd

query, target = "CCOCC", "CCNCC"  # diethyl ether, diethylamine
mces = smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES
connected = smsd.MCS.find(query).match(target)
split = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_fragments().match(target)
large = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_fragments(min_atoms=3).match(target)
edges = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_objective(mces).with_fragments().match(target)

assert connected.best.atom_count == 2
assert split.best.atom_count == 4 and split.best.fragments == ((0, 1), (3, 4))
assert split.best.to_smiles(query) == "CC.CC"
assert not large.found and large.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED
assert large.optimal
assert edges.best.bond_count == 2 and edges.score == 2.0
print("connected MCIS:", connected.best.atom_count, "atoms")
print("fragments MCIS:", split.best.atom_count, "atoms",
      split.best.fragments, split.best.to_smiles(query))
print("fragments of 3 atoms or more:", large.found, large.status.name,
      "| optimal:", large.optimal)
print("fragments MCES:", edges.best.bond_count, "bonds, score", edges.score)

single = smsd.MCS.find("C.O").with_fragments().match("C.O")  # methane, water
none = smsd.MCS.find("C.O").with_objective(mces).with_fragments().match("C.O")
assert single.best.fragments == ((0,), (1,)) and not none.found
print("C.O, MCIS fragments:", single.best.fragments,
      "| MCES found:", none.found)

try:
    smsd.MCS.find(query).with_fragments(min_atoms=0)
except ValueError as error:
    message = str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("min_atoms=0 was accepted")
assert message == "Fragment limits must be positive"
print("min_atoms=0:", message)

The program prints:

connected MCIS: 2 atoms
fragments MCIS: 4 atoms ((0, 1), (3, 4)) CC.CC
fragments of 3 atoms or more: False COMPLETED | optimal: True
fragments MCES: 2 bonds, score 2.0
C.O, MCIS fragments: ((0,), (1,)) | MCES found: False
min_atoms=0: Fragment limits must be positive

A result with no match, COMPLETED status and optimal=True proves that no qualifying common graph exists: here, no pair of fragments of three or more atoms each.

docs.title: Proof, limits and partial results
docs.text:
Three limits stop a search early:

  • timeout_ms: by default the time limit adapts to the size of the pair; 0 stops at once, and a positive value applies to each query and target pair;
  • node_limit: 0, the default, sets no limit; reaching one reports LIMIT_REACHED;
  • cancellation: a CancellationToken whose cancel() can be called from any thread; the search reports CANCELLED. A token cannot be reset, so use a new one for each search.

A stopped search can still return a valid common graph, but it is not proved to be the largest. Describe a result as the maximum only when optimal is true.

import smsd

query = "CC(C)Cc1ccc(cc1)C(C)C(=O)O"  # ibuprofen
target = "COc1ccc2cc(ccc2c1)C(C)C(=O)O"  # naproxen

full = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(2000).match(target)
assert full.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED and full.optimal
assert full.best.atom_count == 14
print("no node limit:", full.status.name, "| optimal:", full.optimal,
      "| atoms:", full.best.atom_count)

rows = []
for limit in (2, 5, 20, 100):
    options = smsd.MCS.Options()
    options.timeout_ms = 2000
    options.node_limit = limit
    result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
    valid = smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, result.best, options) == []
    rows.append((limit, result.status.name, result.optimal,
                 result.best.atom_count, valid))
assert rows == [
    (2, "LIMIT_REACHED", False, 2, True),
    (5, "LIMIT_REACHED", False, 5, True),
    (20, "LIMIT_REACHED", False, 13, True),
    (100, "COMPLETED", True, 14, True),
]
for limit, status, optimal, atoms, valid in rows:
    print(f"node_limit {limit}: {status} | optimal: {optimal} "
          f"| atoms: {atoms} | valid: {valid}")

stopped = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(0).match(target)
token = smsd.CancellationToken()
token.cancel()
options = smsd.MCS.Options()
options.cancellation = token
cancelled = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
for label, result in (("timeout 0", stopped), ("cancelled", cancelled)):
    assert not (result.found or result.optimal or result.complete)
    print(f"{label}: {result.status.name} | found: {result.found}")
assert stopped.status == smsd.SearchStatus.TIMED_OUT
assert cancelled.status == smsd.SearchStatus.CANCELLED

The program prints:

no node limit: COMPLETED | optimal: True | atoms: 14
node_limit 2: LIMIT_REACHED | optimal: False | atoms: 2 | valid: True
node_limit 5: LIMIT_REACHED | optimal: False | atoms: 5 | valid: True
node_limit 20: LIMIT_REACHED | optimal: False | atoms: 13 | valid: True
node_limit 100: COMPLETED | optimal: True | atoms: 14 | valid: True
timeout 0: TIMED_OUT | found: False
cancelled: CANCELLED | found: False

An empty result proves absence only when it is COMPLETED and optimal. An empty result from a stopped search proves nothing.

docs.title: All optimal mappings
docs.text:
match_all(target, limit=1000) returns every optimal mapping, including those related by symmetry, up to limit. When the limit cuts the enumeration short, the status is LIMIT_REACHED with complete=False, while optimal can stay true because the optimum itself is proved. MCS.canonicalize_mapping picks one representative under the symmetries of both molecules, which removes the duplicates.

import smsd

query, target = "C1CC1", "CC(C)C"  # cyclopropane, isobutane
prepared = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(1000)
everything = prepared.match_all(target, limit=100)
capped = prepared.match_all(target, limit=2)

assert len(everything.matches) == 18
assert everything.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED
assert everything.optimal and everything.complete
assert len(capped.matches) == 2
assert capped.status == smsd.SearchStatus.LIMIT_REACHED
assert capped.optimal and not capped.complete
print("limit 100:", len(everything.matches), "mappings,",
      everything.status.name, "| complete:", everything.complete)
print("limit 2:", len(capped.matches), "mappings,", capped.status.name,
      "| optimal:", capped.optimal, "| complete:", capped.complete)

canonical = {
    tuple(sorted(smsd.MCS.canonicalize_mapping(
        query, target, dict(match.atom_mapping)).items()))
    for match in everything.matches
}
assert canonical == {((0, 0), (1, 1))}
print("distinct up to symmetry:", len(canonical), sorted(canonical))

The program prints:

limit 100: 18 mappings, COMPLETED | complete: True
limit 2: 2 mappings, LIMIT_REACHED | optimal: True | complete: False
distinct up to symmetry: 1 [((0, 0), (1, 1))]

docs.title: Chemistry options in an MCS
docs.text:
The rules that decide which atoms and bonds may correspond live in options.chemistry, a ChemOptions object edited in place. Option objects take no keyword arguments; set each field as an attribute. The full table of fields and named profiles is in Chemistry options; this section shows how the main fields change an MCS.

import smsd


def common_atoms(query, target, **fields):
    options = smsd.MCS.Options()
    options.timeout_ms = 1000
    for name, value in fields.items():
        setattr(options.chemistry, name, value)
    result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
    assert result.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED and result.optimal
    return result.best.atom_count if result.found else 0


bond = smsd.BondOrderMode
rows = [
    ("propene, propane: STRICT", common_atoms("C=CC", "CCC")),
    ("propene, propane: LOOSE",
     common_atoms("C=CC", "CCC", match_bond_order=bond.LOOSE)),
    ("propene, propane: ANY",
     common_atoms("C=CC", "CCC", match_bond_order=bond.ANY)),
    ("benzene, cyclohexa-1,3-diene: FLEXIBLE",
     common_atoms("c1ccccc1", "C1=CCCC=C1")),
    ("benzene, cyclohexa-1,3-diene: STRICT",
     common_atoms("c1ccccc1", "C1=CCCC=C1",
                  aromaticity_mode=smsd.AromaticityMode.STRICT)),
    ("acetate, acetic acid: default",
     common_atoms("CC(=O)[O-]", "CC(=O)O")),
    ("acetate, acetic acid: match_formal_charge",
     common_atoms("CC(=O)[O-]", "CC(=O)O", match_formal_charge=True)),
    ("13C and 12C ethanol: default", common_atoms("[13CH3]CO", "[12CH3]CO")),
    ("13C and 12C ethanol: match_isotope",
     common_atoms("[13CH3]CO", "[12CH3]CO", match_isotope=True)),
]
assert [atoms for _, atoms in rows] == [2, 3, 3, 6, 0, 4, 3, 3, 2]
for label, atoms in rows:
    print(f"{label}: {atoms} atoms")

The program prints:

propene, propane: STRICT: 2 atoms
propene, propane: LOOSE: 3 atoms
propene, propane: ANY: 3 atoms
benzene, cyclohexa-1,3-diene: FLEXIBLE: 6 atoms
benzene, cyclohexa-1,3-diene: STRICT: 0 atoms
acetate, acetic acid: default: 4 atoms
acetate, acetic acid: match_formal_charge: 3 atoms
13C and 12C ethanol: default: 3 atoms
13C and 12C ethanol: match_isotope: 2 atoms

BondOrderMode.STRICT, the default, needs equal bond orders; LOOSE and ANY relax that rule. AromaticityMode.FLEXIBLE, the default, lets an aromatic bond match a single or double bond, which is why benzene shares six atoms with cyclohexa-1,3-diene until aromaticity is STRICT. Formal charge and isotope are ignored unless requested; an isotope is compared only where both atoms carry a mass number.

Three ring options restrict how rings may map, and each does so differently:

import smsd


def common_graph(query, target, **fields):
    options = smsd.MCS.Options()
    options.timeout_ms = 1000
    for name, value in fields.items():
        setattr(options.chemistry, name, value)
    result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
    assert result.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED and result.optimal
    if not result.found:
        return 0, ""
    return result.best.atom_count, result.best.to_smiles(query)


naphthalene, styrene = "c1ccc2ccccc2c1", "C=Cc1ccccc1"
rows = [
    ("naphthalene, styrene: default", common_graph(naphthalene, styrene)),
    ("naphthalene, styrene: complete_rings_only",
     common_graph(naphthalene, styrene, complete_rings_only=True)),
    ("naphthalene, styrene: ring_matches_ring_only",
     common_graph(naphthalene, styrene, ring_matches_ring_only=True)),
    ("naphthalene, styrene: ring_fusion_mode STRICT",
     common_graph(naphthalene, styrene,
                  ring_fusion_mode=smsd.RingFusionMode.STRICT)),
    ("cyclohexane, hexane: default", common_graph("C1CCCCC1", "CCCCCC")),
    ("cyclohexane, hexane: ring_matches_ring_only",
     common_graph("C1CCCCC1", "CCCCCC", ring_matches_ring_only=True)),
]
assert [value for _, value in rows] == [
    (8, "C(C)c1ccccc1"), (6, "c1ccccc1"), (6, "c1ccccc1"),
    (6, "C(CCC)CC"), (5, "C(CC)CC"), (0, ""),
]
for label, (atoms, smiles) in rows:
    print(f"{label}: {atoms} atoms {smiles or '(none)'}")

The program prints:

naphthalene, styrene: default: 8 atoms C(C)c1ccccc1
naphthalene, styrene: complete_rings_only: 6 atoms c1ccccc1
naphthalene, styrene: ring_matches_ring_only: 6 atoms c1ccccc1
naphthalene, styrene: ring_fusion_mode STRICT: 6 atoms C(CCC)CC
cyclohexane, hexane: default: 5 atoms C(CC)CC
cyclohexane, hexane: ring_matches_ring_only: 0 atoms (none)
  • complete_rings_only keeps a ring only when the whole ring maps.
  • ring_matches_ring_only lets ring atoms and bonds match only ring atoms and bonds.
  • ring_fusion_mode STRICT needs matched ring atoms to lie in the same number of rings. It does not require complete rings, so the result can be a chain cut from the rings, as above.

Stereochemistry is a hard constraint. With use_chirality or use_bond_stereo, an MCIS search leaves out atoms rather than mapping centres of opposite configuration, and an MCES search drops the fewest bonds. A centre without a stated configuration matches either form.

import smsd


def search(query, target, objective=smsd.MCS.Objective.MCIS, **fields):
    options = smsd.MCS.Options()
    options.timeout_ms = 1000
    options.objective = objective
    for name, value in fields.items():
        setattr(options.chemistry, name, value)
    result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
    assert result.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED and result.optimal
    return result.best.atom_count, result.best.bond_count


l_ala, d_ala = "N[C@@H](C)C(=O)O", "N[C@H](C)C(=O)O"  # L- and D-alanine
trans, cis = "C/C=C/C", "C/C=C\\C"  # trans- and cis-2-butene
r_thf, s_thf = "C[C@@H]1CCCO1", "C[C@H]1CCCO1"  # 2-methyltetrahydrofuran
mces = smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES
rows = [
    ("L-, D-alanine: default", search(l_ala, d_ala)),
    ("L-, D-alanine: use_chirality",
     search(l_ala, d_ala, use_chirality=True)),
    ("trans-, cis-2-butene: default", search(trans, cis)),
    ("trans-, cis-2-butene: use_bond_stereo",
     search(trans, cis, use_bond_stereo=True)),
    ("2-methyltetrahydrofuran enantiomers: MCIS",
     search(r_thf, s_thf, use_chirality=True)),
    ("2-methyltetrahydrofuran enantiomers: MCES",
     search(r_thf, s_thf, mces, use_chirality=True)),
    ("L-alanine, unspecified alanine",
     search(l_ala, "NC(C)C(=O)O", use_chirality=True)),
]
assert [value for _, value in rows] == [
    (6, 5), (5, 4), (4, 3), (3, 2), (5, 5), (6, 5), (6, 5),
]
for label, (atoms, bonds) in rows:
    print(f"{label}: {atoms} atoms, {bonds} bonds")

The program prints:

L-, D-alanine: default: 6 atoms, 5 bonds
L-, D-alanine: use_chirality: 5 atoms, 4 bonds
trans-, cis-2-butene: default: 4 atoms, 3 bonds
trans-, cis-2-butene: use_bond_stereo: 3 atoms, 2 bonds
2-methyltetrahydrofuran enantiomers: MCIS: 5 atoms, 5 bonds
2-methyltetrahydrofuran enantiomers: MCES: 6 atoms, 5 bonds
L-alanine, unspecified alanine: 6 atoms, 5 bonds

Tautomer matching is covered under Tautomers.

docs.title: Atom weights
docs.text:
with_atom_weights(weights) ranks MCIS results by the sum of the weights of the matched query atoms, and then by atoms and bonds. Give exactly one finite weight per query atom, in the query's atom order. score is then in the units of the weights, and a negative weight can make a smaller common graph win. Weights apply to MCIS only.

import math

import smsd

result = smsd.MCS.find("CCO").with_atom_weights([0.5, 1.0, 3.0]).match("CCN")
assert result.score == 1.5 and result.best.atom_count == 2
print("ethanol, ethylamine weighted score:", result.score)

query, target = "OCCCN", "OCC.CCCN"  # 3-aminopropanol; ethanol and propylamine
plain = smsd.MCS.find(query).match(target)
heavy = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_atom_weights([5.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
weighted = heavy.match(target)
negative = smsd.MCS.find("CCO").with_atom_weights([1.0, 1.0, -5.0]).match("CCO")
assert (plain.score, plain.best.to_smiles(query)) == (4.0, "C(CC)N")
assert (weighted.score, weighted.best.to_smiles(query)) == (7.0, "C(C)O")
assert (negative.score, negative.best.to_smiles("CCO")) == (2.0, "CC")
print("unweighted:", plain.score, plain.best.to_smiles(query))
print("oxygen weighted 5:", weighted.score, weighted.best.to_smiles(query))
print("oxygen weighted -5:", negative.score, negative.best.to_smiles("CCO"))

mces = smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES
messages = []
for weights, objective in (([1, 1, 1], mces),
                           ([1, 1], smsd.MCS.Objective.MCIS),
                           ([1, math.nan, 1], smsd.MCS.Objective.MCIS)):
    try:
        smsd.MCS.find("CCO").with_objective(objective).with_atom_weights(weights)
    except ValueError as error:
        messages.append(str(error))
assert messages == [
    "Atom weights are supported only for MCIS",
    "Atom weights must cover every query atom",
    "Atom weights must be finite",
]
for message in messages:
    print("ValueError:", message)

The program prints:

ethanol, ethylamine weighted score: 1.5
unweighted: 4.0 C(CC)N
oxygen weighted 5: 7.0 C(C)O
oxygen weighted -5: 2.0 CC
ValueError: Atom weights are supported only for MCIS
ValueError: Atom weights must cover every query atom
ValueError: Atom weights must be finite

Weights whose positive or negative total is beyond about 2.1 million also raise ValueError. Atom weights cannot be combined with MCS.consensus.

docs.title: Reserved atoms and constrained placement
docs.text:
MCS.Options.excluded_target_atoms makes target atoms unavailable to a search without editing the target. The indices follow the caller's numbering. MCS.match_constrained(queries, target, options=None) places several queries on one target in turn: each search excludes the target atoms that earlier queries used, and the indices in every result refer to the original target.

import smsd

query, target = "CO", "COCCO"  # methanol; 2-methoxyethanol
free = smsd.MCS.find(query).match(target)
options = smsd.MCS.Options()
options.excluded_target_atoms = [3, 4]
reserved = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
assert sorted(free.best.atom_mapping.items()) == [(0, 3), (1, 4)]
assert sorted(reserved.best.atom_mapping.items()) == [(0, 0), (1, 1)]
assert reserved.optimal
print("no exclusions:", sorted(free.best.atom_mapping.items()))
print("atoms 3 and 4 reserved:", sorted(reserved.best.atom_mapping.items()))

placed = smsd.MCS.match_constrained(["CO", "CN"], "CO.CN")
mappings = [sorted(result.best.atom_mapping.items()) for result in placed]
assert mappings == [[(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 2), (1, 3)]]
print("CO, then CN on CO.CN:", mappings)

placed = smsd.MCS.match_constrained(["CC", "CC", "CC"], "CCCC")
mappings = [sorted(result.best.atom_mapping.items()) if result.found else None
            for result in placed]
assert mappings == [[(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 3), (1, 2)], None]
assert all(result.status == smsd.SearchStatus.COMPLETED for result in placed)
print("three CC on butane:", mappings)

The program prints:

no exclusions: [(0, 3), (1, 4)]
atoms 3 and 4 reserved: [(0, 0), (1, 1)]
CO, then CN on CO.CN: [[(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 2), (1, 3)]]
three CC on butane: [[(0, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 3), (1, 2)], None]

Each result is proved optimal for its own query, given the atoms that earlier queries took. In the last case butane has no free pair of bonded carbons left for the third query. The joint placement is not proved optimal and can depend on the order of the queries.

docs.title: Common graph of a series
docs.text:
MCS.consensus(molecules, options=None, threshold=1.0) looks for a common graph present in at least ceil(threshold × len(molecules)) of the inputs, under one shared time limit. The result is an approximate common graph, not proved optimal: optimal is always false, and complete says only that the pass finished. threshold must lie in (0, 1]; atom weights and excluded atoms raise ValueError.

import smsd

series = [
    "c1ccccc1CCN",  # phenethylamine
    "c1ccccc1CCO",  # 2-phenylethanol
    "c1ccccc1CC(=O)O",  # phenylacetic acid
    "Cc1ccccc1CCN",  # 2-methylphenethylamine
]
common = smsd.MCS.consensus(series)
assert common.found and common.to_smiles() == "C(C)c1ccccc1"
assert common.support_count == 4 and common.graph.n == 8
assert not common.optimal and common.complete
assert sorted(common.mappings) == [0, 1, 2, 3]
print("common graph:", common.to_smiles(), "| support:", common.support_count,
      "| optimal:", common.optimal, "| complete:", common.complete)
print("inputs with a mapping:", sorted(common.mappings))

partial = smsd.MCS.consensus(["CCO", "CCN", "O"], threshold=2 / 3)
assert partial.to_smiles() == "CC" and partial.support_count == 2
assert sorted(partial.mappings) == [0, 1]
print("two of three:", partial.to_smiles(), "| supported by", sorted(partial.mappings))

empty = smsd.MCS.consensus([])
assert not empty.found and empty.source_index == -1
print("no inputs:", empty.found, empty.source_index)

The program prints:

common graph: C(C)c1ccccc1 | support: 4 | optimal: False | complete: True
inputs with a mapping: [0, 1, 2, 3]
two of three: CC | supported by [0, 1]
no inputs: False -1

mappings maps each supporting input to a Match from the atoms of graph to that input's atoms. fragment selects the same graph in the input numbered source_index.

docs.title: Validate a mapping
docs.text:
MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, match, options=None) checks a Match or a plain atom mapping against the objective, connectivity, fragment limits, excluded atoms and chemistry, and returns a list of errors; an empty list means the mapping is valid. Without options it applies the default rules, connected MCIS, so validate a result with the options used for the search. Pass the Match itself for an MCES result, because a plain atom mapping selects every compatible bond between the mapped atoms.

import smsd

query, target = "c1ccc(O)cc1", "c1ccc(N)cc1"  # phenol, aniline
best = smsd.MCS.find(query).match(target).best
checks = [
    ("search result", smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, best)),
    ("oxygen on nitrogen", smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, {4: 4})),
    ("target atom twice",
     smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, {0: 0, 1: 0})),
    ("index out of range", smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, {0: 99})),
    ("propane on cyclopropane",
     smsd.MCS.validate_mapping("CCC", "C1CC1", {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 2})),
    ("two ethyl groups",
     smsd.MCS.validate_mapping("CCOCC", "CCNCC", {0: 0, 1: 1, 3: 3, 4: 4})),
]
fragments = smsd.MCS.Options()
fragments.connectivity = smsd.MCS.Connectivity.FRAGMENTS
checks.append(("two ethyl groups, fragments", smsd.MCS.validate_mapping(
    "CCOCC", "CCNCC", {0: 0, 1: 1, 3: 3, 4: 4}, fragments)))

mces = smsd.MCS.Options()
mces.objective = smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES
edges = smsd.MCS.find("C1CC1").with_options(mces).match("CC(C)C").best
checks.append(("MCES result, MCES rules",
               smsd.MCS.validate_mapping("C1CC1", "CC(C)C", edges, mces)))
checks.append(("MCES result, default rules",
               smsd.MCS.validate_mapping("C1CC1", "CC(C)C", edges)))
assert [errors for _, errors in checks] == [
    [], ["Mapped atoms are incompatible"],
    ["Target atom occurs more than once"], ["Mapped atom index out of range"],
    ["Mapped topology is not induced"], ["Selected graph is disconnected"],
    [], [],
    ["Mapped topology is not induced", "MCIS must select every induced bond"],
]
for label, errors in checks:
    print(f"{label}: {errors}")

maximal = smsd.MCS.is_mapping_maximal("CCCO", "CCC.CO", {2: 3, 3: 4})
optimum = smsd.MCS.find("CCCO").match("CCC.CO").best.atom_count
assert maximal and optimum == 3
print("2-atom mapping is maximal:", maximal, "| optimum:", optimum, "atoms")

The program prints:

search result: []
oxygen on nitrogen: ['Mapped atoms are incompatible']
target atom twice: ['Target atom occurs more than once']
index out of range: ['Mapped atom index out of range']
propane on cyclopropane: ['Mapped topology is not induced']
two ethyl groups: ['Selected graph is disconnected']
two ethyl groups, fragments: []
MCES result, MCES rules: []
MCES result, default rules: ['Mapped topology is not induced', 'MCIS must select every induced bond']
2-atom mapping is maximal: True | optimum: 3 atoms

The possible errors are Mapped atom index out of range, Target atom occurs more than once, Mapped target atom is excluded, Mapped atoms are incompatible, Selected bond is outside the atom mapping, Selected bond occurs more than once, Selected bonds are incompatible, Mapped topology is not induced, MCIS must select every induced bond, MCES cannot retain isolated atoms, Selected graph is disconnected, Too many fragments, Fragment is too small, Selected stereochemistry is incompatible and Selected ring is incomplete. An excluded atom index outside the target raises IndexError.

MCS.is_mapping_maximal(query, target, match, options=None) returns true when a valid mapping cannot be extended by any further compatible atom. That is weaker than optimal: the 2-atom mapping above cannot grow, yet the optimum has three atoms. It returns false for an invalid mapping and raises RuntimeError when its proof cannot finish.

docs.title: MCS similarity
docs.text:
The MCS similarity of two molecules is the atom-count Tanimoto of their common graph: common atoms divided by query atoms plus target atoms minus common atoms. No function returns this exact value; compute it from best.atom_count. smsd.similarity_upper_bound(mol1, mol2) returns a fast upper bound on it, and smsd.screen_targets(query, targets, threshold) keeps every target whose bound reaches the threshold, so it never rejects a target that qualifies. Confirm the targets it keeps with an MCS search.

import smsd

query = "c1ccccc1C(=O)O"  # benzoic acid
library = [
    "c1ccccc1C(=O)OC",  # methyl benzoate
    "c1ccc(O)cc1",  # phenol
    "CC(=O)O",  # acetic acid
    "c1ccncc1C(=O)O",  # nicotinic acid
    "CCCC",  # butane
]
prepared = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(1000)
results = prepared.match_many(library, num_threads=1)
query_atoms = smsd.parse_smiles(query).n
exact, bound = [], []
for smiles, result in zip(library, results):
    assert result.optimal
    common = result.best.atom_count if result.found else 0
    target_atoms = smsd.parse_smiles(smiles).n
    exact.append(round(common / (query_atoms + target_atoms - common), 3))
    bound.append(round(smsd.similarity_upper_bound(query, smiles), 3))
assert exact == [0.9, 0.6, 0.444, 0.8, 0.444]
assert bound == [0.9, 0.778, 0.444, 0.8, 0.444]
for smiles, value, limit in zip(library, exact, bound):
    print(f"{smiles:16} MCS similarity {value:.3f} | bound {limit:.3f}")

kept = smsd.screen_targets(query, library, 0.7, num_threads=1)
confirmed = [index for index in kept if exact[index] >= 0.7]
assert kept == [0, 1, 3] and confirmed == [0, 3]
print("bound keeps:", kept, "| MCS confirms:", confirmed)

The program prints:

c1ccccc1C(=O)OC  MCS similarity 0.900 | bound 0.900
c1ccc(O)cc1      MCS similarity 0.600 | bound 0.778
CC(=O)O          MCS similarity 0.444 | bound 0.444
c1ccncc1C(=O)O   MCS similarity 0.800 | bound 0.800
CCCC             MCS similarity 0.444 | bound 0.444
bound keeps: [0, 1, 3] | MCS confirms: [0, 3]

smsd.similarity(mol1, mol2) is the same upper bound, not a fingerprint score. For phenol and aspirin the bound happens to equal the exact MCS similarity, while a fingerprint Tanimoto of the same pair is far lower:

import smsd

phenol, aspirin = "c1ccccc1O", "CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O"
bound = smsd.similarity(phenol, aspirin)
assert bound == smsd.similarity_upper_bound(phenol, aspirin)
result = smsd.MCS.find(phenol).with_timeout(1000).match(aspirin)
assert result.optimal
common = result.best.atom_count
total = smsd.parse_smiles(phenol).n + smsd.parse_smiles(aspirin).n
ecfp4 = smsd.FingerprintOptions.ecfp(radius=2, size=2048)
fingerprint = smsd.tanimoto_coefficient(
    smsd.fingerprint(phenol, options=ecfp4),
    smsd.fingerprint(aspirin, options=ecfp4))
values = (round(bound, 3), round(common / (total - common), 3),
          round(fingerprint, 3))
assert values == (0.538, 0.538, 0.02)
print("smsd.similarity: %.3f | exact MCS similarity: %.3f "
      "| ECFP4 Tanimoto: %.3f" % values)

The program prints:

smsd.similarity: 0.538 | exact MCS similarity: 0.538 | ECFP4 Tanimoto: 0.020

For a screen of a whole library, MCS.match_corpus decides for each target whether its MCS reaches a minimum atom count, and targets that cannot reach it are ruled out before searching, with a proof. See MCS-similarity screen.

docs.title: Export the common graph
docs.text:
Match.to_smiles(query) writes the common graph as SMILES with the cut valences capped, and Match.to_graph(query) returns it as a MolGraph that keeps the original hydrogen counts. The graph can be written as a MOL block with smsd.write_mol_block or drawn with smsd.depict_svg.

import smsd

query, target = "C1CC1", "CC(C)C"  # cyclopropane, isobutane
edges = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_objective(smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES)
best = edges.match(target).best
graph = best.to_graph(query)
counts = smsd.write_mol_block(graph).splitlines()[3]
assert best.to_smiles(query) == "C(C)C"
assert smsd.to_smiles(graph) == "[CH2]C[CH2]"
assert counts.split()[:2] == ["3", "2"]
print("to_smiles:", best.to_smiles(query))
print("to_graph:", smsd.to_smiles(graph))
print("MOL block atoms and bonds:", counts.split()[:2])

The program prints:

to_smiles: C(C)C
to_graph: [CH2]C[CH2]
MOL block atoms and bonds: ['3', '2']

match_with_smarts(target) runs the search and returns a SmartsResult with the result and the common graph as a SMARTS pattern under the query's chemistry; the pattern is empty when nothing is found. The pattern can then search a library. Under the default FLEXIBLE aromaticity its bonds also match single and double bonds, so a benzene pattern finds cyclohexane; choose AromaticityMode.STRICT for an aromatic-only pattern. Stereo, tautomer, complete-ring and strict ring-fusion rules cannot be written as SMARTS, so they raise ValueError rather than being dropped.

import smsd

library = ["c1ccccc1O", "c1ccccc1N", "Cc1ccccc1", "CCO", "C1CCCCC1"]
exported = smsd.MCS.find("c1ccccc1O").with_timeout(1000).match_with_smarts(
    "c1ccccc1N")  # phenol, aniline
pattern = exported.smarts
assert exported.result.optimal
assert pattern == "[#6]-,=,:1-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]1"
search = smsd.Substructure.smarts(pattern).with_timeout(1000)
hits = [smiles for smiles, result
        in zip(library, search.match_many(library, num_threads=1))
        if result.found]
assert hits == ["c1ccccc1O", "c1ccccc1N", "Cc1ccccc1", "C1CCCCC1"]
print("pattern:", pattern)
print("library hits:", hits)

strict = smsd.MCS.Options()
strict.chemistry.aromaticity_mode = smsd.AromaticityMode.STRICT
aromatic = smsd.MCS.find("c1ccccc1O").with_options(strict).match_with_smarts(
    "c1ccccc1N").smarts
assert aromatic == "[#6;a]:1:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]1"
print("STRICT aromaticity:", aromatic)

stereo = smsd.MCS.Options()
stereo.chemistry.use_chirality = True
try:
    smsd.MCS.find("N[C@@H](C)C(=O)O").with_options(stereo).match_with_smarts(
        "N[C@@H](C)C(=O)O")
except ValueError as error:
    message = str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("a chiral SMARTS export was accepted")
assert message == ("SMARTS export cannot represent these stereo, tautomer or "
                   "ring constraints")
print("use_chirality:", message)

nothing = smsd.MCS.find("O").match_with_smarts("C")
assert nothing.smarts == "" and not nothing.result.found
print("no common atom:", repr(nothing.smarts))

The program prints:

pattern: [#6]-,=,:1-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]-,=,:[#6]1
library hits: ['c1ccccc1O', 'c1ccccc1N', 'Cc1ccccc1', 'C1CCCCC1']
STRICT aromaticity: [#6;a]:1:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]:[#6;a]1
use_chirality: SMARTS export cannot represent these stereo, tautomer or ring constraints
no common atom: ''

The pattern carries neither the induced rule of MCIS nor the proof of the search. Writing patterns by hand is covered in SMARTS queries.

docs.title: Draw the result
docs.text:
smsd.highlight.mcs_svg(query, target, result, *, opts=None, **kwargs) draws both molecules with the common graph highlighted, without RDKit and without a new search. It takes the SearchResult, not a Match, and records the status, optimal and complete in the SVG, both as attributes of the root element and in its title, so a figure cannot hide a stopped search. Import it from smsd.highlight; import smsd alone does not provide it. Keyword arguments are the fields of smsd.DepictOptions, such as width and height.

import re
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import smsd
from smsd.highlight import mcs_svg

query, target = "c1ccccc1O", "c1ccccc1N"  # phenol, aniline
result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_timeout(1000).match(target)
svg = mcs_svg(query, target, result, width=600, height=300)
title = re.search(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", svg).group(1)
flags = re.findall(r'data-(search-status|optimal|complete)="(\w+)"', svg)
assert title == ("MCS: 6 mapped atoms; status COMPLETED; optimal true; "
                 "complete true")
assert flags == [("search-status", "COMPLETED"), ("optimal", "true"),
                 ("complete", "true")]
print(title)
print(flags)

with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "phenol_aniline.svg"
    smsd.save_svg(svg, path)
    assert path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == svg
    print("saved", path.name)

try:
    mcs_svg(query, target, result.best)
except TypeError as error:
    message = str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("a Match was accepted")
assert message == "result must be a SearchResult"
print("TypeError:", message)

The program prints:

MCS: 6 mapped atoms; status COMPLETED; optimal true; complete true
[('search-status', 'COMPLETED'), ('optimal', 'true'), ('complete', 'true')]
saved phenol_aniline.svg
TypeError: result must be a SearchResult

An MCES result can leave out a bond between two mapped atoms, which the pair drawing cannot show, so mcs_svg raises ValueError for it. Draw the selected graph from to_graph instead:

import smsd
from smsd.highlight import mcs_svg

query, target = "C1CC1", "CC(C)C"  # cyclopropane, isobutane
edges = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_objective(smsd.MCS.Objective.MCES)
result = edges.match(target)
try:
    mcs_svg(query, target, result)
except ValueError:
    rejected = True
else:
    rejected = False
svg = smsd.depict_svg(result.best.to_graph(query), width=300, height=200)
assert rejected and "<svg" in svg
print("mcs_svg rejects the MCES result:", rejected)
print("selected graph drawn:", "<svg" in svg)

The program prints:

mcs_svg rejects the MCES result: True
selected graph drawn: True

smsd.depict_pair(mol1, mol2, mapping) draws two molecules with any mapping from atoms of mol1 to atoms of mol2 highlighted, and smsd.depict_mapping(mol, mapping) highlights the keys of a mapping on one molecule, so invert an MCS mapping to highlight target atoms. Both return native SVG. smsd.depict_mcs(mol1, mol2, *, tautomer_aware=False, timeout_ms=10000, size=(600, 300)) returns an image drawn with RDKit. It runs its own MCIS search and shows no status, so prefer mcs_svg for any figure that should state whether the result is proved. Its highlight_color argument has no effect and is deprecated. The drawing options are listed under Depiction.

docs.title: Tautomers
docs.text:
With tautomer_aware, atoms and bonds that differ only by the position of a mobile hydrogen can correspond. Such matches usually also need a relaxed bond order, so ChemOptions.tautomer_profile() sets tautomer_aware with BondOrderMode.LOOSE.

import smsd

query = smsd.parse_smiles("ONC(C)=O")  # acetohydroxamic acid
target = smsd.parse_smiles("ON=C(C)O")  # its imidic acid tautomer
options = smsd.MCS.Options()
options.timeout_ms = 1000
options.chemistry = smsd.ChemOptions.tautomer_profile()
result = smsd.MCS.find(query).with_options(options).match(target)
match = result.best
assert result.optimal and match.atom_count == 5
assert smsd.MCS.validate_tautomer_consistency(query, target, match)
print("common atoms:", match.atom_count, "| optimal:", result.optimal)
print("protons conserved:",
      smsd.MCS.validate_tautomer_consistency(query, target, match))

scores = []
for pH in (2.0, 7.4, 9.0, 12.0):
    chemistry = smsd.ChemOptions.tautomer_profile().with_ph(pH)
    score = smsd.MCS.compute_tautomer_confidence(query, target, match, chemistry)
    scores.append((pH, round(score, 3)))
assert scores == [(2.0, 0.85), (7.4, 0.829), (9.0, 0.425), (12.0, 0.1)]
for pH, score in scores:
    print(f"pH {pH}: confidence {score}")

keto = smsd.MCS.Options()
keto.chemistry.tautomer_aware = True
keto.chemistry.match_bond_order = smsd.BondOrderMode.ANY
default = smsd.MCS.find("CC(=O)C").match("CC(O)=C")  # acetone, its enol
relaxed = smsd.MCS.find("CC(=O)C").with_options(keto).match("CC(O)=C")
assert (default.best.atom_count, relaxed.best.atom_count) == (2, 4)
print("acetone, prop-1-en-2-ol:", default.best.atom_count, "atoms by default,",
      relaxed.best.atom_count, "with tautomer_aware and ANY")

The program prints:

common atoms: 5 | optimal: True
protons conserved: True
pH 2.0: confidence 0.85
pH 7.4: confidence 0.829
pH 9.0: confidence 0.425
pH 12.0: confidence 0.1
acetone, prop-1-en-2-ol: 2 atoms by default, 4 with tautomer_aware and ANY

MCS.validate_tautomer_consistency(query, target, match) reports whether a Match or atom mapping conserves the mobile N–H, O–H and S–H protons of each mapped tautomeric group. MCS.compute_tautomer_confidence(query, target, match, chemistry) scores the tautomeric relaxations a Match uses at the pH and solvent of chemistry. The score is a heuristic in [0, 1], not a probability, and it changes neither the molecules nor the search. It needs a Match; a plain atom mapping raises TypeError.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
MCS methods:

Method Returns MCS.find(query) A prepared query with MCS.Options() with_options(options) A new query holding a copy of options with_timeout(milliseconds) A new query with that time limit; negative selects the adaptive limit with_objective(objective) A new query with MCS.Objective.MCIS or MCES with_fragments(*, min_atoms=1, max_fragments=2147483647) A new query allowing fragments with_atom_weights(weights) A new MCIS query ranked by atom weights match(target) A SearchResult with at most one Match match_all(target, limit=1000) Every optimal mapping up to limit match_many(targets, *, num_threads=0) One SearchResult per target, in order, each with its own time limit match_with_smarts(target) A SmartsResult(result, smarts) match_corpus(corpus, minimum_atoms, *, gpu_prefilter=False, num_threads=0) One CorpusSearchResult per target of a TargetCorpus MCS.validate_mapping(query, target, match, options=None) A list of errors, empty when valid MCS.is_mapping_maximal(query, target, match, options=None) Whether no compatible extension exists MCS.canonicalize_mapping(query, target, atom_mapping) The representative mapping under both molecules' symmetries MCS.validate_tautomer_consistency(query, target, match) Whether mobile protons are conserved MCS.compute_tautomer_confidence(query, target, match, chemistry) A heuristic score in [0, 1] MCS.match_constrained(queries, target, options=None) One SearchResult per query, in order MCS.consensus(molecules, options=None, threshold=1.0) A ConsensusResult

num_threads=0 uses the OpenMP default, which OMP_NUM_THREADS sets; a negative value raises ValueError. limit must be positive.

MCS.Options fields:

Field Type Default Meaning chemistry ChemOptions ChemOptions() Atom and bond matching rules timeout_ms int -1 Time limit per pair in milliseconds; negative selects min(30,000, 500 + 2 × query atoms × target atoms); 0 stops at once node_limit int 0 Search nodes allowed; 0 sets no limit cancellation CancellationToken or None None Stops the search with CANCELLED once cancelled objective MCS.Objective MCIS MCIS maximises atoms, MCES maximises bonds connectivity MCS.Connectivity CONNECTED CONNECTED or FRAGMENTS min_fragment_atoms int 1 Smallest fragment allowed with FRAGMENTS max_fragments int 2147483647 Most fragments allowed with FRAGMENTS atom_weights list[float] [] One weight per query atom; MCIS only excluded_target_atoms list[int] [] Target atoms unavailable to the search

The default time limit is 1.3 s for two 20-atom molecules, 5.5 s for two 50-atom molecules and 30 s from 122 atoms each. Parsing and preparation fall outside it.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Report status, optimal and complete together with any result. A stopped search can return a valid but smaller common graph, or none.
  • Scores mean atoms for MCIS, bonds for MCES and weight units with atom weights; never compare them across objectives.
  • Tied optimal mappings are not ranked chemically. A stopped MCIS search can return a different mapping in another language or version, so do not rely on the exact mapping of a stopped search.
  • MCES declines very large pairs before searching, with LIMIT_REACHED and no match; see Size limits.
  • with_options copies the options when it is called, so later edits to the options object do not reach the prepared query. A CancellationToken is shared, however.
  • Other entry points use their own bounded defaults: the find_mcs molecular tool uses 1,000 ms and 100,000 nodes, the command-line --timeout is 10,000 ms per pair, and depict_mcs uses 10,000 ms.
  • The MCS search always runs on the CPU. match_corpus(..., gpu_prefilter=True) affects only the step that rules out targets before searching; see Request the GPU for a corpus pre-screen.
  • R-group decomposition needs the whole core in every target, so it is a substructure operation; see R-group decomposition.
